    Chapter 1 · Lecture 2

    Multi-Armed Bandits

    One state, kkk actions, noisy rewards. With states and delayed credit removed, the problem that remains is exploration against exploitation, plus the update rule that every later chapter reuses.

    one state, k arms

    The setting

    In full RL an action changes the reward, the next state and the data you will see later. A bandit keeps only the first: choose AtA_tAt​, observe RtR_tRt​, repeat. There are no state transitions and no delayed credit assignment. The exploration–exploitation dilemma is still there.

    Evaluative vs. instructive feedback

    Supervised learning gives instructive feedback: the correct label, independent of what you predicted. RL gives evaluative feedback: how good the action you took was, and nothing about the actions you did not take. Counterfactuals are missing, so an action you never try is an action whose value you never learn.

    k-armed bandit

    Actions a∈{1,…,k}a \in \{1,\dots,k\}a∈{1,…,k}. At each step select AtA_tAt​ and receive RtR_tRt​. The true action value is

    q∗(a)≐E[Rt∣At=a].q_*(a) \doteq \E[R_t \mid A_t = a].q∗​(a)≐E[Rt​∣At​=a].
    We maintain estimates Qt(a)≈q∗(a)Q_t(a) \approx q_*(a)Qt​(a)≈q∗​(a) and want to maximize cumulative reward ∑tRt\sum_t R_t∑t​Rt​. Two jobs: estimation (learn values from data) and control (decide which arm to sample next).

    Sample averages and ε-greedy

    With Nt(a)N_t(a)Nt​(a) the number of times aaa was chosen before ttt, the sample-average estimate is

    Qt(a)=∑i=1t−1Ri 1{Ai=a}∑i=1t−11{Ai=a}=1Nt(a)∑i<t: Ai=aRi.Q_t(a) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{t-1} R_i\,\mathbb 1\{A_i = a\}}{\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\mathbb 1\{A_i = a\}} = \frac{1}{N_t(a)}\sum_{i<t:\,A_i=a} R_i .Qt​(a)=∑i=1t−1​1{Ai​=a}∑i=1t−1​Ri​1{Ai​=a}​=Nt​(a)1​i<t:Ai​=a∑​Ri​.

    In a stationary problem Qt(a)→q∗(a)Q_t(a) \to q_*(a)Qt​(a)→q∗​(a) by the law of large numbers, provided aaa keeps being sampled. Estimation is rarely the bottleneck. The bottleneck is collecting informative data for the right arms.

    Greedy picks At=arg max⁡aQt(a)A_t = \argmax_a Q_t(a)At​=argmaxa​Qt​(a) (ties broken randomly). It fails because the data distribution depends on the algorithm: an early unlucky draw makes a good arm look bad, greedy stops pulling it, and its estimate stops improving.

    Worked example

    k=2k = 2k=2, Q1=(0,0)Q_1 = (0,0)Q1​=(0,0), ε=0.2\varepsilon = 0.2ε=0.2. Pull arm 1, get 1: Q(1)=1Q(1) = 1Q(1)=1. Pull arm 1, get 0: Q(1)=0.5Q(1) = 0.5Q(1)=0.5. Pull arm 2, get 2: Q(2)=2Q(2) = 2Q(2)=2. At step 4 arm 2 is greedy, so Pr⁡(arm 2)=0.8+0.2/2=0.9\Pr(\text{arm }2) = 0.8 + 0.2/2 = 0.9Pr(arm 2)=0.8+0.2/2=0.9 and Pr⁡(arm 1)=0.1\Pr(\text{arm }1) = 0.1Pr(arm 1)=0.1.

    Evaluating methods. One bandit instance can favour a method by luck, so methods are compared on the 10-armed testbed: for each run draw q∗(a)∼N(0,1)q_*(a) \sim \mathcal N(0,1)q∗​(a)∼N(0,1), rewards Rt∼N(q∗(At),1)R_t \sim \mathcal N(q_*(A_t), 1)Rt​∼N(q∗​(At​),1), run 1000 steps, average curves over many runs. Two metrics: average reward and % optimal action. Greedy looks good early. ε-greedy wins later because it cannot lock in permanently.

    Incremental updates and nonstationarity

    Averaging the 100th number does not require re-summing 99. For one arm, with QnQ_nQn​ the mean of its first n−1n-1n−1 rewards:

    Qn+1=1n∑i=1nRi=1n((n−1)Qn+Rn)=Qn+1n(Rn−Qn).Q_{n+1} = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n R_i = \frac1n\Big((n-1)Q_n + R_n\Big) = Q_n + \frac1n\big(R_n - Q_n\big).Qn+1​=n1​i=1∑n​Ri​=n1​((n−1)Qn​+Rn​)=Qn​+n1​(Rn​−Qn​).
    The universal update template
    new←old+α (target−old)\text{new} \leftarrow \text{old} + \alpha\,(\text{target} - \text{old})new←old+α(target−old)

    Target = what we move toward, (target−old)(\text{target} - \text{old})(target−old) = prediction error, α\alphaα = step size. MC, TD, Q-learning, semi-gradient TD and actor–critic are all this line with a different target.

    Sample averages weight all past rewards equally, which is right when q∗q_*q∗​ is fixed and wrong when it drifts. In a nonstationary problem we want tracking, not convergence. Use a constant step size α∈(0,1]\alpha \in (0,1]α∈(0,1]:

    Qn+1=Qn+α(Rn−Qn)=(1−α)Qn+αRn=(1−α)nQ1+∑i=1nα(1−α)n−iRi.Q_{n+1} = Q_n + \alpha(R_n - Q_n) = (1-\alpha)Q_n + \alpha R_n = (1-\alpha)^n Q_1 + \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha(1-\alpha)^{n-i} R_i .Qn+1​=Qn​+α(Rn​−Qn​)=(1−α)Qn​+αRn​=(1−α)nQ1​+i=1∑n​α(1−α)n−iRi​.

    Older rewards get exponentially smaller weight: an exponential recency-weighted average. The weights sum to one, (1−α)n+∑i=1nα(1−α)n−i=1(1-\alpha)^n + \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha(1-\alpha)^{n-i} = 1(1−α)n+∑i=1n​α(1−α)n−i=1, so it is a genuine weighted average that includes the initial guess Q1Q_1Q1​.

    Step-size conditions (stochastic approximation)

    A step-size sequence αn(a)\alpha_n(a)αn​(a) makes the estimate converge with probability 1 to q∗(a)q_*(a)q∗​(a) (stationary case) if

    ∑n=1∞αn=∞and∑n=1∞αn2<∞.\sum_{n=1}^\infty \alpha_n = \infty \qquad\text{and}\qquad \sum_{n=1}^\infty \alpha_n^2 < \infty .n=1∑∞​αn​=∞andn=1∑∞​αn2​<∞.
    The first condition makes steps large enough to overcome initial conditions and noise; the second makes them shrink enough to converge. αn=1/n\alpha_n = 1/nαn​=1/n satisfies both. A constant α\alphaα violates the second: the estimate never settles, which is exactly what you want when q∗q_*q∗​ moves.

    Optimism and upper confidence bounds

    Optimistic initial values. Set Q1(a)=Q0Q_1(a) = Q_0Q1​(a)=Q0​ well above any plausible reward. A purely greedy agent then tries every arm, because each tried arm disappoints and drops below the untried ones. Exploration comes from the initialization, not the policy. It is mostly a one-time effect: if the environment changes later, the optimism does not come back.

    Why ε-greedy is crude. It explores uniformly, ignoring both how close an arm is to the best and how uncertain its estimate is. Better: explore where uncertainty is large.

    Upper confidence bound (UCB) action selection
    At=arg max⁡a[ Qt(a)+cln⁡tNt(a) ],A_t = \argmax_a \left[\,Q_t(a) + c\sqrt{\frac{\ln t}{N_t(a)}}\,\right],At​=aargmax​[Qt​(a)+cNt​(a)lnt​​],

    with an arm having Nt(a)=0N_t(a) = 0Nt​(a)=0 treated as maximizing. The bonus shrinks when aaa is pulled (Nt(a)N_t(a)Nt​(a) grows) and slowly rises when it is ignored (ln⁡t\ln tlnt grows). UCB explores in a directed way: plausible and under-tested arms get priority, and over time it concentrates on the good ones.

    Gradient bandits: the first policy gradient

    Instead of estimating values and acting nearly greedily, parameterize the policy directly. Keep preferences Ht(a)∈RH_t(a) \in \RHt​(a)∈R and act by softmax:

    πt(a)≐Pr⁡(At=a)=eHt(a)∑b=1keHt(b).\pi_t(a) \doteq \Pr(A_t = a) = \frac{e^{H_t(a)}}{\sum_{b=1}^k e^{H_t(b)}} .πt​(a)≐Pr(At​=a)=∑b=1k​eHt​(b)eHt​(a)​.

    Every action keeps positive probability, and adding the same constant to all preferences changes nothing. The objective is expected reward,

    J(H)=E[R]=∑x=1kπ(x) q∗(x),H(a)←H(a)+α ∂J∂H(a).J(H) = \E[R] = \sum_{x=1}^k \pi(x)\, q_*(x), \qquad H(a) \leftarrow H(a) + \alpha\,\frac{\partial J}{\partial H(a)} .J(H)=E[R]=x=1∑k​π(x)q∗​(x),H(a)←H(a)+α∂H(a)∂J​.
    Softmax derivative and the exact gradient

    The softmax Jacobian is ∂π(x)∂H(a)=π(x)(1{x=a}−π(a))\dfrac{\partial \pi(x)}{\partial H(a)} = \pi(x)\big(\mathbb 1\{x=a\} - \pi(a)\big)∂H(a)∂π(x)​=π(x)(1{x=a}−π(a)). By the chain rule

    ∂J∂H(a)=∑xq∗(x) π(x)(1{x=a}−π(a))=π(a)q∗(a)−π(a)∑xπ(x)q∗(x)=π(a)(q∗(a)−J).\frac{\partial J}{\partial H(a)} = \sum_x q_*(x)\,\pi(x)\big(\mathbb 1\{x=a\} - \pi(a)\big) = \pi(a)q_*(a) - \pi(a)\sum_x \pi(x)q_*(x) = \pi(a)\big(q_*(a) - J\big).∂H(a)∂J​=x∑​q∗​(x)π(x)(1{x=a}−π(a))=π(a)q∗​(a)−π(a)x∑​π(x)q∗​(x)=π(a)(q∗​(a)−J).

    Raise the preference of actions that beat the policy's average, lower the rest. Written as an expectation over A∼πA \sim \piA∼π,

    ∂J∂H(a)=EA∼π[q∗(A)(1{A=a}−π(a))],\frac{\partial J}{\partial H(a)} = \E_{A\sim\pi}\Big[q_*(A)\big(\mathbb 1\{A = a\} - \pi(a)\big)\Big],∂H(a)∂J​=EA∼π​[q∗​(A)(1{A=a}−π(a))],

    which can be sampled: since E[Rt∣At]=q∗(At)\E[R_t \mid A_t] = q_*(A_t)E[Rt​∣At​]=q∗​(At​), the quantity Rt(1{At=a}−πt(a))R_t(\mathbb 1\{A_t = a\} - \pi_t(a))Rt​(1{At​=a}−πt​(a)) is an unbiased gradient estimate.

    Gradient-bandit update (with baseline)
    Ht+1(a)=Ht(a)+α (Rt−Rˉt)(1{At=a}−πt(a))H_{t+1}(a) = H_t(a) + \alpha\,(R_t - \bar R_t)\big(\mathbb 1\{A_t = a\} - \pi_t(a)\big)Ht+1​(a)=Ht​(a)+α(Rt​−Rˉt​)(1{At​=a}−πt​(a))

    Chosen action: H(At)+=α(Rt−Rˉt)(1−πt(At))H(A_t) \mathrel{+}= \alpha(R_t - \bar R_t)(1 - \pi_t(A_t))H(At​)+=α(Rt​−Rˉt​)(1−πt​(At​)). Others: H(a)−=α(Rt−Rˉt)πt(a)H(a) \mathrel{-}= \alpha(R_t - \bar R_t)\pi_t(a)H(a)−=α(Rt​−Rˉt​)πt​(a). The baseline Rˉt\bar R_tRˉt​ is a running average of past rewards.

    Why a baseline is free. For any constant BBB, ∑xB ∂π(x)/∂H(a)=B ∂(∑xπ(x))/∂H(a)=0\sum_x B\,\partial\pi(x)/\partial H(a) = B\,\partial(\sum_x\pi(x))/\partial H(a) = 0∑x​B∂π(x)/∂H(a)=B∂(∑x​π(x))/∂H(a)=0, so subtracting it leaves the expected gradient unchanged while reducing variance. This is the same argument as REINFORCE with baseline in Chapter 9.

    Contextual bandits

    Each round now comes with a context sts_tst​, and the policy is π(a∣s)\pi(a \mid s)π(a∣s). Different contexts can have different best actions. It is still not full RL: the action affects the immediate reward but not the next context. Once actions change the future state distribution, planning through time matters (Chapter 2).

    What is context worth?

    Case A: (q∗(1),q∗(2))=(10,20)(q_*(1), q_*(2)) = (10, 20)(q∗​(1),q∗​(2))=(10,20). Case B: (90,80)(90, 80)(90,80). Each with probability 1/21/21/2. Without seeing the case, both arms give E[R]=50\E[R] = 50E[R]=50. Seeing it, pick arm 2 in A and arm 1 in B: E[R]=0.5⋅20+0.5⋅90=55\E[R] = 0.5\cdot 20 + 0.5\cdot 90 = 55E[R]=0.5⋅20+0.5⋅90=55. Observing context raises the achievable reward because the policy can specialize.

    Lab: the 10-armed testbed

    LabTestbed simulation

    Each run draws a fresh bandit and runs every selected method on it, so the comparisons share randomness. Switch to the nonstationary setting to see sample averages fall behind a constant step size.

    Reference implementation

    import numpy as np

class Bandit:
    """k-armed testbed: q*(a) ~ N(0,1), R ~ N(q*(A), 1). Optional random-walk drift."""
    def __init__(self, k=10, drift=0.0, rng=None):
        self.rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
        self.k, self.drift = k, drift
        self.q = np.zeros(k) if drift else self.rng.normal(0, 1, k)

    def pull(self, a):
        r = self.rng.normal(self.q[a], 1.0)
        if self.drift:                       # nonstationary: q* takes a random walk
            self.q += self.rng.normal(0, self.drift, self.k)
        return r

def argmax_random(x, rng):
    return rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(x == x.max()))

def run_value_method(bandit, steps, eps=0.1, alpha=None, q0=0.0, ucb_c=None, rng=None):
    """eps-greedy / optimistic / UCB with sample-average (alpha=None) or constant alpha."""
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    k = bandit.k
    Q, N = np.full(k, q0, float), np.zeros(k)
    rewards, optimal = np.zeros(steps), np.zeros(steps)
    for t in range(steps):
        if ucb_c is not None:
            if (N == 0).any():
                a = rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(N == 0))
            else:
                a = argmax_random(Q + ucb_c * np.sqrt(np.log(t + 1) / N), rng)
        elif rng.random() < eps:
            a = rng.integers(k)
        else:
            a = argmax_random(Q, rng)
        best = bandit.q.argmax()              # read before the drift step
        r = bandit.pull(a)
        N[a] += 1
        step = 1.0 / N[a] if alpha is None else alpha
        Q[a] += step * (r - Q[a])             # new = old + step * (target - old)
        rewards[t], optimal[t] = r, a == best
    return rewards, optimal

def run_gradient_bandit(bandit, steps, alpha=0.1, baseline=True, rng=None):
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    H = np.zeros(bandit.k)
    r_bar, rewards, optimal = 0.0, np.zeros(steps), np.zeros(steps)
    for t in range(steps):
        pi = np.exp(H - H.max()); pi /= pi.sum()          # stable softmax
        a = rng.choice(bandit.k, p=pi)
        best = bandit.q.argmax()
        r = bandit.pull(a)
        b = r_bar if baseline else 0.0
        one_hot = np.zeros(bandit.k); one_hot[a] = 1.0
        H += alpha * (r - b) * (one_hot - pi)              # sampled gradient ascent
        r_bar += (r - r_bar) / (t + 1)                     # baseline excludes R_t itself
        rewards[t], optimal[t] = r, a == best
    return rewards, optimal

if __name__ == "__main__":
    runs, steps = 500, 1000
    curves = {}
    for name, kw in {"greedy": dict(eps=0.0), "eps=0.1": dict(eps=0.1),
                     "UCB c=2": dict(ucb_c=2.0), "optimistic Q0=5": dict(eps=0.0, q0=5.0, alpha=0.1)}.items():
        R = np.zeros(steps)
        for i in range(runs):
            r, _ = run_value_method(Bandit(rng=np.random.default_rng(i)), steps, **kw,
                                    rng=np.random.default_rng(10_000 + i))
            R += r
        curves[name] = R / runs
    for name, c in curves.items():
        print(f"{name:18s} mean reward over last 100 steps: {c[-100:].mean():.3f}")

    Gotchas and fine print

    LLN needs infinitely many samples per arm

    "Sample averages converge" holds only for arms that keep being pulled. Under greedy selection an arm can be abandoned after one unlucky reward, and its estimate freezes forever. That is the formal reason greedy can lock in.

    Fixed ε caps asymptotic performance

    Even with perfect estimates, ε-greedy picks the best arm with probability only 1−ε+ε/k1 - \varepsilon + \varepsilon/k1−ε+ε/k: 91% for ε=0.1\varepsilon = 0.1ε=0.1, k=10k = 10k=10. Its regret grows linearly in ttt. To be asymptotically optimal ε must decay.

    Optimism with α = 1/n lasts exactly one pull

    With sample averages the first reward replaces Q1Q_1Q1​ entirely (Q2=Q1+1⋅(R1−Q1)=R1Q_2 = Q_1 + 1\cdot(R_1 - Q_1) = R_1Q2​=Q1​+1⋅(R1​−Q1​)=R1​), so the optimistic initial value is forgotten after one pull of each arm. The lasting optimism in the textbook figure comes from a constant α=0.1\alpha = 0.1α=0.1, where Q1Q_1Q1​ decays as (1−α)n(1-\alpha)^n(1−α)n.

    Constant α is biased toward Q1Q_1Q1​

    The weight on Q1Q_1Q1​ is (1−α)n(1-\alpha)^n(1−α)n: the estimate is biased for any finite nnn, but the bias vanishes geometrically. Sample averages are unbiased from the first pull because Q1Q_1Q1​ gets weight zero.

    UCB's constant c is a heuristic here

    The logarithmic-regret guarantee belongs to UCB1 with bounded rewards in [0,1][0,1][0,1] and c=2c = \sqrt 2c=2​ (Auer et al., 2002). With Gaussian rewards and a hand-picked ccc it is a well-motivated heuristic. UCB is also hard to extend to nonstationary problems and large state spaces, which is why it mostly stays in bandits (but reappears inside MCTS in Chapter 7).

    The baseline may not depend on the current action

    Subtracting BBB is unbiased because ∑x∂π(x)/∂H(a)=0\sum_x \partial\pi(x)/\partial H(a) = 0∑x​∂π(x)/∂H(a)=0 for a constant BBB. A baseline that depends on AtA_tAt​ breaks this. A running average that includes RtR_tRt​ itself is slightly correlated with AtA_tAt​; excluding RtR_tRt​ (as in the code) avoids the issue. Without any baseline, shifting all rewards by +4+4+4 makes learning much slower, though the expected gradient is unchanged: the variance is what changes.

    Regret, the standard yardstick

    Not on the slides but standard: RegretT=Tmax⁡aq∗(a)−∑t=1TE[Rt]\text{Regret}_T = T\max_a q_*(a) - \sum_{t=1}^T \E[R_t]RegretT​=Tmaxa​q∗​(a)−∑t=1T​E[Rt​]. Fixed-ε greedy has linear regret; UCB1 achieves O(log⁡T)O(\log T)O(logT), which matches the Lai–Robbins lower bound up to constants.

    Self-test

    Why is exploration unavoidable in RL but not in supervised learning?

    Supervised feedback is instructive: you learn the correct answer whatever you predicted. RL feedback is evaluative: you only learn the reward of the action you took. Without trying an action you get no data about it, so some actions must be taken partly for information.

    ε = 0.1, k = 10. What is the probability of choosing the greedy arm, and of one specific non-greedy arm?

    Greedy: 1−0.1+0.1/10=0.911 - 0.1 + 0.1/10 = 0.911−0.1+0.1/10=0.91. A specific other arm: 0.1/10=0.010.1/10 = 0.010.1/10=0.01. (Assuming a unique greedy arm.)

    Derive Qn+1=Qn+1n(Rn−Qn)Q_{n+1} = Q_n + \frac1n(R_n - Q_n)Qn+1​=Qn​+n1​(Rn​−Qn​) from the definition of the sample mean.

    Qn+1=1n∑i=1nRi=1n(∑i=1n−1Ri+Rn)=1n((n−1)Qn+Rn)=Qn+1n(Rn−Qn)Q_{n+1} = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n R_i = \frac1n\big(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}R_i + R_n\big) = \frac1n\big((n-1)Q_n + R_n\big) = Q_n + \frac1n(R_n - Q_n)Qn+1​=n1​∑i=1n​Ri​=n1​(∑i=1n−1​Ri​+Rn​)=n1​((n−1)Qn​+Rn​)=Qn​+n1​(Rn​−Qn​).

    With constant α = 0.5 and Q1=0Q_1 = 0Q1​=0, rewards 4, 0, 2 arrive. What is Q4Q_4Q4​, and what weight does each reward get?

    Q2=2Q_2 = 2Q2​=2, Q3=1Q_3 = 1Q3​=1, Q4=1.5Q_4 = 1.5Q4​=1.5. Weights α(1−α)n−i\alpha(1-\alpha)^{n-i}α(1−α)n−i with n=3n=3n=3: R1R_1R1​ gets 0.1250.1250.125, R2R_2R2​ gets 0.250.250.25, R3R_3R3​ gets 0.50.50.5, and Q1Q_1Q1​ gets (0.5)3=0.125(0.5)^3 = 0.125(0.5)3=0.125. Check: 0.125⋅4+0.25⋅0+0.5⋅2=1.50.125\cdot 4 + 0.25\cdot 0 + 0.5\cdot 2 = 1.50.125⋅4+0.25⋅0+0.5⋅2=1.5.

    Which of α = 1/n, α = 0.1, α = 1/√n satisfy the Robbins–Monro conditions?

    1/n1/n1/n: ∑1/n=∞\sum 1/n = \infty∑1/n=∞, ∑1/n2<∞\sum 1/n^2 < \infty∑1/n2<∞, yes. 0.10.10.1: ∑0.01=∞\sum 0.01 = \infty∑0.01=∞, fails the second condition. 1/n1/\sqrt n1/n​: ∑1/n=∞\sum 1/\sqrt n = \infty∑1/n​=∞ and ∑1/n=∞\sum 1/n = \infty∑1/n=∞, fails the second condition too.

    UCB: an arm was pulled 4 times at t = 100 and another 25 times. With c = 2 and equal Q, which is preferred, and by how much?

    Why does optimistic initialization help little in a nonstationary bandit?

    Its exploration is driven by the initial values only. Once every arm has been tried enough, the optimism has decayed away and the agent behaves greedily. If q∗q_*q∗​ changes later, nothing pushes it to re-test arms it has written off.

    A contextual bandit vs. an MDP: what is the one structural difference?

    In a contextual bandit the action affects only the immediate reward; the next context is drawn independently of it. In an MDP the action also affects the distribution of the next state, so current choices change future opportunities and credit must be assigned through time.

    Chapter 2 · Lecture 3

    Finite Markov Decision Processes

    Reward and return

    Reward hypothesis

    All goals can be described as maximizing the expected cumulative sum of a scalar reward. Reward says what to achieve, not how. Rewarding a proxy (e.g. capturing pieces instead of winning) invites the agent to exploit the proxy.

    Lab: Bellman equations on a gridworld

    Lab5 × 5 gridworld (Sutton & Barto, Example 3.5)

    Every action from A gives +10 and teleports to A′; from B it gives +5 and teleports to B′. Bumping into the edge costs −1, all other moves give 0. Values are computed exactly: a linear solve for vπv_\pivπ​, value iteration for v∗v_*v∗​. Click any cell to see its Bellman equation with the numbers filled in.

    Reference implementation

    import numpy as np

N, GAMMA = 5, 0.9
A, A_PRIME, B, B_PRIME = (0, 1), (4, 1), (0, 3), (2, 3)
MOVES = [(-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)]           # N, S, E, W

def step(s, a):
    """Deterministic dynamics: returns (s', r)."""
    if s == A: return A_PRIME, 10.0
    if s == B: return B_PRIME, 5.0
    r, c = s[0] + MOVES[a][0], s[1] + MOVES[a][1]
    if 0 <= r < N and 0 <= c < N:
        return (r, c), 0.0
    return s, -1.0                                     # bump: stay, pay -1

idx = lambda s: s[0] * N + s[1]
states = [(r, c) for r in range(N) for c in range(N)]

def evaluate_random_policy():
    """Solve v = r_pi + gamma P_pi v exactly."""
    P, r = np.zeros((N * N, N * N)), np.zeros(N * N)
    for s in states:
        for a in range(4):
            s2, rew = step(s, a)
            P[idx(s), idx(s2)] += 0.25
            r[idx(s)] += 0.25 * rew
    return np.linalg.solve(np.eye(N * N) - GAMMA * P, r).reshape(N, N)

def value_iteration(tol=1e-10):
    v = np.zeros(N * N)
    while True:
        v_new = np.array([max(rew + GAMMA * v[idx(s2)] for s2, rew in (step(s, a) for a in range(4)))
                          for s in states])
        if np.abs(v_new - v).max() < tol:
            return v_new.reshape(N, N)
        v = v_new

print(np.round(evaluate_random_policy(), 1))   # A ~ 8.8, B ~ 5.3
print(np.round(value_iteration(), 1))          # A ~ 24.4

    Gotchas and fine print

    A single optimal policy is a theorem, not a definition

    Control asks for one π∗\pi_*π∗​ that maximizes vπ(s)v_\pi(s)vπ​(s) at every state simultaneously. Since ⪰\succeq⪰ is only a partial order, that is not automatic. For finite discounted MDPs it is a theorem, and the optimum is attained by a deterministic stationary policy.

    Why v∗v_*v∗​ is unique

    The optimality operator (T∗u)(s)=max⁡a∑s′,rp(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γu(s′)](T_*u)(s) = \max_a\sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s,a)[r + \gamma u(s')](T∗​u)(s)=maxa​∑s′,r​p(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γu(s′)] is a γ\gammaγ-contraction in the sup norm, ∥T∗u−T∗w∥∞≤γ∥u−w∥∞\|T_*u - T_*w\|_\infty \le \gamma\|u - w\|_\infty∥T∗​u−T∗​w∥∞​≤γ∥u−w∥∞​. Banach's fixed-point theorem gives a unique fixed point and convergence of iterating T∗T_*T∗​ (value iteration). Same argument for TπT_\piTπ​. Optimal policies can be non-unique; v∗v_*v∗​ and q∗q_*q∗​ cannot.

    Linear vs. nonlinear

    The expectation equations are linear in vπv_\pivπ​, so they have a closed-form solution. The optimality equations contain a max and are nonlinear: no closed form, hence iterative methods.

    Why action values matter for model-free control

    Greedy action selection from v∗v_*v∗​ needs ppp to do the one-step lookahead. Greedy selection from q∗q_*q∗​ is a table lookup. That is the real reason later model-free control methods (MC control, Sarsa, Q-learning) learn qqq instead of vvv.

    Discounting in the gridworld example

    In the lab, A has value about 8.8 under the random policy even though it pays +10 immediately: after teleporting to A′ on the bottom edge, the random walk keeps bumping into the wall at −1. B pays only +5 but is worth slightly more than 5, because B′ sits away from the edge.

    Self-test

    γ = 0.5, rewards R1=2R_1 = 2R1​=2, R2=1R_2 = 1R2​=1, R3=4R_3 = 4R3​=4, then termination. Compute G0G_0G0​, G1G_1G1​, G2G_2G2​.

    Work backwards with Gt=Rt+1+γGt+1G_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma G_{t+1}Gt​=Rt+1​+γGt+1​: G2=4G_2 = 4G2​=4, G1=1+0.5⋅4=3G_1 = 1 + 0.5\cdot 4 = 3G1​=1+0.5⋅4=3, G0=2+0.5⋅3=3.5G_0 = 2 + 0.5\cdot 3 = 3.5G0​=2+0.5⋅3=3.5.

    Constant reward +1 forever with γ = 0.9. What is GtG_tGt​?

    ∑k0.9k=1/(1−0.9)=10\sum_k 0.9^k = 1/(1-0.9) = 10∑k​0.9k=1/(1−0.9)=10.

    Is the Markov property a property of the environment or of the state signal?

    Of the state signal. The same physical system can be Markov under one representation (position and velocity) and non-Markov under another (position only).

    Write qπq_\piqπ​ in terms of vπv_\pivπ​, and vπv_\pivπ​ in terms of qπq_\piqπ​.

    qπ(s,a)=∑s′,rp(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γvπ(s′)]q_\pi(s,a) = \sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s,a)[r + \gamma v_\pi(s')]qπ​(s,a)=∑s′,r​p(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γvπ​(s′)] and vπ(s)=∑aπ(a∣s)qπ(s,a)v_\pi(s) = \sum_a\pi(a\mid s)q_\pi(s,a)vπ​(s)=∑a​π(a∣s)qπ​(s,a).

    Which step in the Bellman derivation uses the Markov property?

    Replacing Eπ[Gt+1∣St,At,St+1=s′,Rt+1]\E_\pi[G_{t+1}\mid S_t, A_t, S_{t+1}=s', R_{t+1}]Eπ​[Gt+1​∣St​,At​,St+1​=s′,Rt+1​] by Eπ[Gt+1∣St+1=s′]=vπ(s′)\E_\pi[G_{t+1}\mid S_{t+1}=s'] = v_\pi(s')Eπ​[Gt+1​∣St+1​=s′]=vπ​(s′): the future after s′s's′ must not depend on how we got there.

    Adding a constant c to every reward in a continuing task: what happens to vπv_\pivπ​? Does it matter in an episodic task?

    Continuing: every value shifts by c/(1−γ)c/(1-\gamma)c/(1−γ), which does not change the ordering of policies. Episodic: the shift is ccc times the expected remaining (discounted) episode length, which depends on the policy. A positive ccc can make the agent prefer long episodes, a negative one short episodes, so it can change the optimal policy.

    Two actions in s: q∗(s,a1)=3q_*(s,a_1) = 3q∗​(s,a1​)=3, q∗(s,a2)=7q_*(s,a_2) = 7q∗​(s,a2​)=7. What is v∗(s)v_*(s)v∗​(s) and what does an optimal policy do in s?

    v∗(s)=max⁡aq∗(s,a)=7v_*(s) = \max_a q_*(s,a) = 7v∗​(s)=maxa​q∗​(s,a)=7; any optimal policy picks a2a_2a2​ in sss (with probability 1, since there is no tie).

    Why can't you write v∗v_*v∗​ in closed form like vπ=(I−γPπ)−1rπv_\pi = (I-\gamma P_\pi)^{-1}r_\pivπ​=(I−γPπ​)−1rπ​?

    The max in the optimality equation makes it nonlinear; there is no single matrix PPP to invert because which action is chosen depends on v∗v_*v∗​ itself. You need iterative methods (value or policy iteration) or a linear program.

    Chapter 3 · Lecture 4

    Dynamic Programming

    Planning with a known model. Turn the Bellman equations into update rules, alternate evaluation and improvement, and arrive at policy iteration, value iteration and the GPI pattern behind every later control method.

    expected update

    Setting

    Assume a finite MDP with bounded rewards and known dynamics p(s′,r∣s,a)p(s',r\mid s,a)p(s′,r∣s,a). Because the model is known, expectations are computed exactly: these are expected updates, unlike the sampled updates of Monte Carlo and TD.

    The template is to repeat two steps: evaluation π→vπ\pi \to v_\piπ→vπ​ (how good is the policy?) and improvement vπ→π′v_\pi \to \pi'vπ​→π′ (can we act better?). Every DP update also bootstraps: it builds a new estimate of V(s)V(s)V(s) from current estimates V(s′)V(s')V(s′). The same principle drives TD, Sarsa and Q-learning.

    Policy improvement

    The one-step deviation value qπ(s,a)=∑s′,rp(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γvπ(s′)]q_\pi(s,a) = \sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s,a)[r + \gamma v_\pi(s')]qπ​(s,a)=∑s′,r​p(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γvπ​(s′)] means: take aaa once, then follow π\piπ. If qπ(s,a)>vπ(s)q_\pi(s,a) > v_\pi(s)qπ​(s,a)>vπ​(s), deviating once at sss helps.

    Policy improvement theorem

    If qπ(s,π′(s))≥vπ(s)q_\pi(s, \pi'(s)) \ge v_\pi(s)qπ​(s,π′(s))≥vπ​(s) for all sss, then vπ′(s)≥vπ(s)v_{\pi'}(s) \ge v_\pi(s)vπ′​(s)≥vπ​(s) for all sss. Strict inequality at some sss in the hypothesis gives strict inequality there in the conclusion.

    Proof (unroll, replacing one more π\piπ-step by a π′\pi'π′-step each time):

    vπ(s)≤qπ(s,π′(s))=Eπ′[Rt+1+γvπ(St+1)∣St=s]≤Eπ′[Rt+1+γqπ(St+1,π′(St+1))∣St=s]=Eπ′[Rt+1+γRt+2+γ2vπ(St+2)∣St=s]≤⋯≤Eπ′[Rt+1+γRt+2+γ2Rt+3+⋯∣St=s]=vπ′(s).\begin{aligned} v_\pi(s) &\le q_\pi(s,\pi'(s)) = \E_{\pi'}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1}) \mid S_t = s\big]\\ &\le \E_{\pi'}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma q_\pi(S_{t+1}, \pi'(S_{t+1})) \mid S_t = s\big]\\ &= \E_{\pi'}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 v_\pi(S_{t+2}) \mid S_t = s\big]\\ &\le \cdots \le \E_{\pi'}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2R_{t+3} + \cdots \mid S_t = s\big] = v_{\pi'}(s). \end{aligned}vπ​(s)​≤qπ​(s,π′(s))=Eπ′​[Rt+1​+γvπ​(St+1​)∣St​=s]≤Eπ′​[Rt+1​+γqπ​(St+1​,π′(St+1​))∣St​=s]=Eπ′​[Rt+1​+γRt+2​+γ2vπ​(St+2​)∣St​=s]≤⋯≤Eπ′​[Rt+1​+γRt+2​+γ2Rt+3​+⋯∣St​=s]=vπ′​(s).​

    The hypothesis must hold at all states, because after one step the agent can land anywhere.

Then v∗(s)v_*(s)v∗​(s) is the maximal probability of reaching 100 from sss. Try it in the second lab.

    Asynchronous DP and the cost of DP

    Cost. Brute-force policy search faces knk^nkn deterministic policies. DP is polynomial: one sweep of expected backups costs O(n2k)O(n^2k)O(n2k) with dense dynamics. But the state space itself suffers the curse of dimensionality: ddd variables with mmm values each give n=mdn = m^dn=md states (backgammon: over 102010^{20}1020). Even one sweep can be infeasible.

    Asynchronous DP backs up selected states in any order, e.g. V(sk)←max⁡a∑s′,rp(s′,r∣sk,a)[r+γV(s′)]V(s_k) \leftarrow \max_a\sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s_k,a)[r + \gamma V(s')]V(sk​)←maxa​∑s′,r​p(s′,r∣sk​,a)[r+γV(s′)]. For γ<1\gamma < 1γ<1 it converges if every state is backed up infinitely often. It lets you focus computation on relevant states and interleave planning with real interaction, which leads to sampled, online RL updates.

    Generalized policy iteration

    Two interacting processes: evaluation V⇝vπV \rightsquigarrow v_\piV⇝vπ​ and improvement π⇝greedy(V)\pi \rightsquigarrow \text{greedy}(V)π⇝greedy(V). They need not strictly alternate. They are stable together only when VVV is consistent with π\piπ and π\piπ is greedy with respect to VVV, which is exactly the Bellman optimality equation: (π∗,v∗)(\pi_*, v_*)(π∗​,v∗​). Most RL algorithms are approximate GPI. The DP backup averages over all successors with ppp; the RL backup uses one sampled target Rt+1+γV(St+1)R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1})Rt+1​+γV(St+1​).

    LabValue iteration on the gambler's problem

    Change the coin and the tie-breaking rule. The value function does not depend on tie-breaking; the plotted "optimal policy" does.

    Reference implementation

    import numpy as np

# A tabular MDP as arrays: P[s, a, s'] transition probs, R[s, a] expected reward.
# Terminal states: rows of P that are all zero (or self-loops with R = 0).

def policy_evaluation(P, R, pi, gamma=1.0, theta=1e-8, in_place=True):
    """pi[s, a] = probability. Returns v_pi by iterative sweeps."""
    nS = P.shape[0]
    V = np.zeros(nS)
    while True:
        delta = 0.0
        V_old = V if in_place else V.copy()
        for s in range(nS):
            v = np.sum(pi[s] * (R[s] + gamma * P[s] @ V_old))
            delta = max(delta, abs(v - V[s]))
            V[s] = v
        if delta < theta:
            return V

def greedy(P, R, V, gamma):
    Q = R + gamma * np.einsum("sat,t->sa", P, V)
    return np.eye(P.shape[1])[Q.argmax(axis=1)], Q    # one-hot deterministic policy

def policy_iteration(P, R, gamma=0.9):
    nS, nA = R.shape
    pi = np.full((nS, nA), 1.0 / nA)
    while True:
        V = policy_evaluation(P, R, pi, gamma)
        new_pi, Q = greedy(P, R, V, gamma)
        # stop on stable *values*, not on argmax labels: ties can make labels flip forever
        if np.allclose(np.sum(new_pi * Q, 1), np.sum(pi * Q, 1), atol=1e-10):
            return new_pi, V
        pi = new_pi

def value_iteration(P, R, gamma=0.9, theta=1e-10):
    V = np.zeros(P.shape[0])
    while True:
        Q = R + gamma * np.einsum("sat,t->sa", P, V)
        V_new = Q.max(axis=1)
        if np.abs(V_new - V).max() < theta:
            return greedy(P, R, V_new, gamma)[0], V_new
        V = V_new

def gambler(p_h=0.4, goal=100, theta=1e-12):
    V = np.zeros(goal + 1); V[goal] = 1.0          # terminal value 1 encodes the +1 reward
    while True:
        delta = 0.0
        for s in range(1, goal):
            stakes = np.arange(0, min(s, goal - s) + 1)
            v = np.max(p_h * V[s + stakes] + (1 - p_h) * V[s - stakes])
            delta = max(delta, abs(v - V[s])); V[s] = v
        if delta < theta:
            break
    policy = np.zeros(goal + 1, int)
    for s in range(1, goal):
        stakes = np.arange(1, min(s, goal - s) + 1)
        q = p_h * V[s + stakes] + (1 - p_h) * V[s - stakes]
        policy[s] = stakes[np.flatnonzero(q >= q.max() - 1e-9)[0]]   # smallest maximizing stake
    return V, policy

    Gotchas and fine print

    The stopping rule bounds the step, not the error

    Δ<θ\Delta < \thetaΔ<θ is about consecutive iterates. For a γ\gammaγ-contraction, ∥vk+1−vk∥∞<θ\|v_{k+1} - v_k\|_\infty < \theta∥vk+1​−vk​∥∞​<θ implies ∥vk+1−v⋆∥∞≤γθ/(1−γ)\|v_{k+1} - v^\star\|_\infty \le \gamma\theta/(1-\gamma)∥vk+1​−v⋆∥∞​≤γθ/(1−γ), which blows up as γ→1\gamma \to 1γ→1. For VI, if ∥V−v∗∥∞≤ε\|V - v_*\|_\infty \le \varepsilon∥V−v∗​∥∞​≤ε, the greedy policy satisfies ∥vπ−v∗∥∞≤2γε/(1−γ)\|v_\pi - v_*\|_\infty \le 2\gamma\varepsilon/(1-\gamma)∥vπ​−v∗​∥∞​≤2γε/(1−γ).

    Both running examples have γ = 1

    The gridworld (−14,−20,−22-14, -20, -22−14,−20,−22) and the gambler use γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1, where the contraction argument does not apply. What saves them is termination: with terminal states removed, PπP_\piPπ​ is substochastic, and if π\piπ terminates with probability 1 from every state (a proper policy) its spectral radius is below 1. Improper policies break this: staking 0 forever never terminates. That is harmless in the gambler because all rewards are 0, but with −1 per step such a policy has value −∞-\infty−∞.

    PI's stopping test can cycle

    "Stop if the policy is unchanged" fails when actions tie and ties are broken arbitrarily: the policy can flip between equally good actions forever. Fix: change an action only if the new one is strictly better, or stop when vπv_\pivπ​ stops changing (as in the code).

    Termination of PI needs strictness

    "Finitely many policies + monotone improvement" alone does not prove PI stops at the optimum. You also need that a non-optimal π\piπ is always strictly improved somewhere, which is the "improvement stalls ⇒ optimal" argument.

    The gambler's optimal policy is not unique

    The slides omit php_hph​ (the textbook uses 0.40.40.4). For a subfair coin, bold play (stake min⁡(s,100−s)\min(s, 100-s)min(s,100−s)) is optimal, and there are many ties. The spiky textbook plot is one optimal policy, selected by tie-breaking toward the smallest stake. Switch the tie-breaking in the lab to see a different, equally optimal policy.

    GPI is a pattern, not a theorem

    "Evaluation and improvement can be interleaved in many ways" does not mean every interleaving converges. Convergence is proved per scheme (PI, VI, modified PI, asynchronous VI with infinitely-often updates). With approximation and sampling it can fail.

    "VI is often faster" depends on the problem

    PI usually needs very few iterations but each needs a full evaluation. VI needs about log⁡(1/ε)/log⁡(1/γ)\log(1/\varepsilon)/\log(1/\gamma)log(1/ε)/log(1/γ) cheap sweeps, which gets slow as γ→1\gamma \to 1γ→1.

    Self-test

    4 × 4 gridworld, random policy, γ = 1, v0=0v_0 = 0v0​=0. What is v1v_1v1​ for every non-terminal state, and v2v_2v2​ for the state next to a terminal?

    v1=−1v_1 = -1v1​=−1 everywhere (one step of reward −1, successor values 0). For the neighbour of a terminal, three moves lead to non-terminal states with v1=−1v_1 = -1v1​=−1 (including bumping back to itself if it is on the edge) and one move enters the terminal with value 0: v2=−1+14(−1−1−1+0)=−1.75v_2 = -1 + \tfrac14(-1-1-1+0) = -1.75v2​=−1+41​(−1−1−1+0)=−1.75.

    In-place vs. two-array evaluation: same answer? Same speed?

    Same fixed point vπv_\pivπ​. In-place usually converges in fewer sweeps because later states in a sweep already see updated values, but its speed depends on the sweep order.

    Why must the policy-improvement hypothesis hold at every state, not just at s?

    The proof unrolls vπ(St+1)v_\pi(S_{t+1})vπ​(St+1​), vπ(St+2)v_\pi(S_{t+2})vπ​(St+2​), … at whatever states the new policy visits. If the inequality failed at a reachable state, the chain of inequalities would break there.

    VI vs. PI: which does fewer iterations and which does less work per iteration?

    PI typically needs very few outer iterations but each includes a full policy evaluation. VI does one sweep per iteration (cheap) but needs many iterations, especially when γ is close to 1.

    γ = 0.9, θ = 0.01. If VI stops when Δ < θ, how far can V be from v* in sup norm?

    At most γθ/(1−γ)=0.9⋅0.01/0.1=0.09\gamma\theta/(1-\gamma) = 0.9\cdot0.01/0.1 = 0.09γθ/(1−γ)=0.9⋅0.01/0.1=0.09.

    What does asynchronous DP require for convergence, and why is that interesting?

    Every state must be backed up infinitely often (with γ<1\gamma<1γ<1). The order is otherwise free, which allows focusing on relevant states and mixing planning with real experience. That freedom is what RTDP, prioritized sweeping and Dyna exploit in Chapter 7.

    In GPI, why is the pair (π*, v*) the only stable point?

    Stability needs V=vπV = v_\piV=vπ​ (evaluation does nothing) and π\piπ greedy w.r.t. VVV (improvement does nothing). Together: vπ(s)=max⁡a∑p[r+γvπ(s′)]v_\pi(s) = \max_a\sum p[r + \gamma v_\pi(s')]vπ​(s)=maxa​∑p[r+γvπ​(s′)], the Bellman optimality equation, whose unique solution is v∗v_*v∗​.

    Gambler with ph=0.4p_h = 0.4ph​=0.4: what is v∗(50)v_*(50)v∗​(50)?

    Stake everything: win with probability 0.40.40.4. No policy does better from 50, so v∗(50)=0.4v_*(50) = 0.4v∗​(50)=0.4. (Check it in the lab: hover the value curve at 50.)

    Chapter 4 · Lecture 5

    Monte Carlo Methods

    Drop the model. Estimate values by averaging the returns of complete sampled episodes, learn action values so improvement needs no model, and use importance sampling to learn about one policy from another's data.

    full sampled episode

    Setting

    Monte Carlo (MC) is model-free estimation from complete episodes. No p(s′,r∣s,a)p(s',r\mid s,a)p(s′,r∣s,a) is needed: values are estimated straight from the definition,

    vπ(s)=Eπ[Gt∣St=s]  ≈  1n∑i=1nG(i)(s),v_\pi(s) = \E_\pi[G_t\mid S_t = s] \;\approx\; \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n G^{(i)}(s),vπ​(s)=Eπ​[Gt​∣St​=s]≈n1​i=1∑n​G(i)(s),

    by averaging returns observed after visits to sss. This needs episodic tasks (every episode terminates with probability 1), with Gt=∑k=0T−t−1γkRt+k+1G_t = \sum_{k=0}^{T-t-1}\gamma^kR_{t+k+1}Gt​=∑k=0T−t−1​γkRt+k+1​.

    No bootstrapping. The target is the realized return GtG_tGt​, never another estimate V(s′)V(s')V(s′). Each state learns only from its own returns.

    MethodModel?Bootstraps?Update when
    DPyesyesplanning sweeps, expected one-step backups
    MCnonoafter the episode ends
    TDnoyesafter each sampled step

    MC strengths: unbiased targets, simple, model-free, cost per state independent of ∣S∣|\S|∣S∣. Weaknesses: must wait for episode end, higher variance than bootstrapping.

    MC prediction

    • Every-visit MC uses all of Gt1,…,GtmG_{t_1},\dots,G_{t_m}Gt1​​,…,Gtm​​.

    Convergence of first-visit MC

    First-visit returns to sss from independent episodes are i.i.d. with mean vπ(s)v_\pi(s)vπ​(s), so by the strong law V(s)→vπ(s)V(s) \to v_\pi(s)V(s)→vπ​(s) almost surely as N(s)→∞N(s) \to \inftyN(s)→∞, with standard error σ/N(s)\sigma/\sqrt{N(s)}σ/N(s)​. Why i.i.d. with the right mean: the first visit time is a stopping time, and the strong Markov property says the process after it is a fresh copy started at sss.

    Blackjack. State == = (player sum 12–21, dealer's showing card, usable ace), actions hit/stick, reward +1/0/−1+1/0/-1+1/0/−1 at the end, γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1. So every GtG_tGt​ equals the final outcome. Computing ppp for blackjack by hand is painful; sampling episodes is easy. The first lab below runs it.

    Labs: blackjack and infinite variance

    LabBlackjack by first-visit Monte Carlo

    Infinite deck, dealer sticks on 17 or more. Prediction evaluates the policy "stick only on 20 or 21". Control runs Monte Carlo with exploring starts and shows v∗v_*v∗​ and the learned policy. Hover a cell for its value and visit count.

    LabOrdinary vs. weighted importance sampling

    One state, two actions. right ends the episode with reward 0. left returns to the state with probability 0.9 and ends with +1 with probability 0.1. The target policy always goes left, so vπ(s)=1v_\pi(s) = 1vπ​(s)=1. The behavior policy picks each action with probability ½. Ten independent runs of each estimator, log-scaled episode axis.

    Reference implementation

    import numpy as np
from collections import defaultdict

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def draw():                       # infinite deck: A=1, face cards count 10
    return min(rng.integers(1, 14), 10)

def hand_value(cards):
    s, usable = sum(cards), 1 in cards and sum(cards) + 10 <= 21
    return (s + 10 if usable else s), usable

def play(policy, state0=None, action0=None):
    """One blackjack episode. Returns [(state, action)], final reward (gamma = 1)."""
    if state0 is None:
        player, dealer = [draw(), draw()], [draw(), draw()]
        while hand_value(player)[0] < 12:
            player.append(draw())
    else:                                          # exploring start
        total, dealer_show, usable = state0
        player = [1, total - 11] if usable else [10, total - 10]
        dealer = [dealer_show, draw()]
    traj, a = [], action0
    while True:
        total, usable = hand_value(player)
        s = (total, dealer[0], usable)
        if a is None:
            a = policy(s)
        traj.append((s, a))
        if a == 0:                                 # stick
            break
        player.append(draw())
        if hand_value(player)[0] > 21:
            return traj, -1.0
        a = None
    while hand_value(dealer)[0] < 17:
        dealer.append(draw())
    p, d = hand_value(player)[0], hand_value(dealer)[0]
    return traj, float(d > 21 or p > d) - float(d <= 21 and d > p)

def first_visit_mc_prediction(policy, episodes=500_000):
    V, N = defaultdict(float), defaultdict(int)
    for _ in range(episodes):
        traj, G = play(policy)                     # gamma = 1: every G_t equals the outcome
        for s in {s for s, _ in traj}:             # states never repeat in blackjack
            N[s] += 1
            V[s] += (G - V[s]) / N[s]
    return V

def mc_exploring_starts(episodes=500_000):
    Q, N = defaultdict(float), defaultdict(int)
    pi = lambda s: int(Q[(s, 1)] > Q[(s, 0)]) if (s, 0) in Q or (s, 1) in Q else int(s[0] < 20)
    for _ in range(episodes):
        s0 = (rng.integers(12, 22), rng.integers(1, 11), bool(rng.integers(2)))
        traj, G = play(pi, s0, int(rng.integers(2)))
        for s, a in dict.fromkeys(traj):           # first visit of each pair, in order
            N[(s, a)] += 1
            Q[(s, a)] += (G - Q[(s, a)]) / N[(s, a)]
    return Q

def off_policy_weighted_is(target, behavior_probs, episodes, gen_episode):
    """Incremental weighted IS for V^pi. gen_episode() -> [(s, a, r), ...] under b."""
    V, C = defaultdict(float), defaultdict(float)
    for _ in range(episodes):
        ep, G, W = gen_episode(), 0.0, 1.0
        for s, a, r in reversed(ep):               # every-visit, backward accumulation
            G = r + G                              # gamma = 1
            W *= target(a, s) / behavior_probs(a, s)
            if W == 0.0:
                break
            C[s] += W
            V[s] += (W / C[s]) * (G - V[s])
    return V

V = first_visit_mc_prediction(lambda s: int(s[0] < 20), 100_000)
print(round(V[(13, 2, False)], 3), round(V[(20, 10, False)], 3))

    Gotchas and fine print

    ε-greedy control converges to the best ε-soft policy, not π*

    The theorem guarantees monotone improvement inside the ε-soft class; vπ′=vπv_{\pi'} = v_\pivπ′​=vπ​ holds iff π\piπ is optimal among ε-soft policies. Reaching π∗\pi_*π∗​ needs ε→0\varepsilon \to 0ε→0 under GLIE: every pair visited infinitely often, greedy in the limit (e.g. εk=1/k\varepsilon_k = 1/kεk​=1/k).

    The theorem needs the same ε

    The decomposition of π\piπ requires π(a∣s)≥ε/∣A(s)∣\pi(a\mid s) \ge \varepsilon/|\A(s)|π(a∣s)≥ε/∣A(s)∣ with the ε that π′\pi'π′ uses. If ε shrinks between iterations, qπ(s,π′)≥vπ(s)q_\pi(s,\pi') \ge v_\pi(s)qπ​(s,π′)≥vπ​(s) is no longer guaranteed.

    The algorithm does not satisfy the theorem's hypotheses

    The theorem assumes the exact qπq_\piqπ​. MC control improves after every episode, and QQQ averages returns from a sequence of different policies, so it is nobody's qπq_\piqπ​. This is approximate GPI. (For the exploring-starts variant, general convergence was long an open problem.)

    "Unbiased" means first-visit with a fixed policy

    Every-visit MC is biased in finite samples (returns within an episode are correlated and the number of visits is random) but still consistent. Every-visit pools across episodes: (sum of all visit returns)/(total visits), not a mean of per-episode means.

    In blackjack, first-visit = every-visit

    No state repeats within an episode: the player sum only grows, or the usable ace switches to non-usable.

    MC is more robust to non-Markov states than bootstrapping

    It estimates E[Gt∣St=s]\E[G_t\mid S_t = s]E[Gt​∣St​=s] directly and never uses v(s)=E[R+γv(S′)]v(s) = \E[R + \gamma v(S')]v(s)=E[R+γv(S′)], which is the step that needs the Markov property.

    Weighted IS after one sample

    With one nonzero-weight sample, weighted IS returns exactly that sample's GGG, whatever its weight. So in small samples it is biased toward returns observed under bbb. In the one-state example ordinary IS has infinite variance while weighted IS is exactly right after the first nonzero-weight episode.

    "TD(∞) ≡ MC" mixes notations

    In nnn-step TD, MC is the n→∞n \to \inftyn→∞ limit. In TD(λ\lambdaλ) it is λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1 (exactly so for the offline version).

    Self-test

    γ = 1. Episode: s → x → s → terminal with rewards 1, 0, 3. First-visit and every-visit estimates of V(s) after this one episode?

    G0=1+0+3=4G_0 = 1 + 0 + 3 = 4G0​=1+0+3=4, G2=3G_2 = 3G2​=3. First-visit: 4. Every-visit: (4+3)/2=3.5(4+3)/2 = 3.5(4+3)/2=3.5.

    Why does MC control learn Q instead of V?

    Greedy improvement from VVV requires a one-step lookahead through ppp. From QQQ it is arg max⁡aQ(s,a)\argmax_a Q(s,a)argmaxa​Q(s,a), which needs no model.

    3 actions, ε = 0.3. Probabilities under ε-greedy?

    Greedy: 1−0.3+0.1=0.81 - 0.3 + 0.1 = 0.81−0.3+0.1=0.8; each other action: 0.10.10.1.

    Why do the transition probabilities cancel in the importance ratio?

    The probability of a trajectory under either policy is ∏kπ(Ak∣Sk)p(Sk+1∣Sk,Ak)\prod_k \pi(A_k\mid S_k)p(S_{k+1}\mid S_k,A_k)∏k​π(Ak​∣Sk​)p(Sk+1​∣Sk​,Ak​) vs. the same with bbb. The environment terms are identical in numerator and denominator because the environment does not depend on the policy.

    Target π is greedy (deterministic), b is uniform over 2 actions. An episode of 4 steps where b happened to take the greedy action each time. What is ρ for t = 0?

    Each factor is 1/0.5=21/0.5 = 21/0.5=2, so ρ0:3=24=16\rho_{0:3} = 2^4 = 16ρ0:3​=24=16. Had bbb taken a non-greedy action at any step, ρ0:3=0\rho_{0:3} = 0ρ0:3​=0.

    Ordinary vs. weighted IS: which would you pick in practice and why?

    Usually weighted IS: its variance is bounded when returns are bounded and it converges much faster. Ordinary IS is unbiased but can have huge or infinite variance. Weighted IS is biased, though the bias vanishes asymptotically.

    Why is off-policy MC control with a greedy target slow on long episodes?

    Only the tail of each episode after the last non-greedy (exploratory) action contributes; earlier steps get weight 0. With long episodes and frequent exploration, very few steps carry information.

    When might you prefer MC over TD even though TD is often faster?

    When the state signal is not Markov (MC does not rely on the Bellman recursion), when you need unbiased estimates, or when episodes are short and cheap. MC also does not propagate errors from bad estimates of other states.

    Chapter 5 · Lecture 6

    Temporal-Difference Learning

    Sample like Monte Carlo, bootstrap like dynamic programming. Learn a guess from a guess after every step, then turn it into control with Sarsa, Q-learning and Double Q-learning.

    one sampled step + bootstrap

    The central idea

    TD learning combines the MC idea (learn from raw experience, no model) with the DP idea (bootstrap: update toward an estimate built from other estimates). MC waits for the full return GtG_tGt​; TD updates immediately toward Rt+1+γV(St+1)R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1})Rt+1​+γV(St+1​).

    MethodSource of estimateBackup
    DPmodel + bootstrapfull expectation, one step
    MCsamples, no bootstrapcomplete sampled return
    TDsamples + bootstrapone sampled step

    All three estimate vπ(s)=Eπ[Gt∣St=s]v_\pi(s) = \E_\pi[G_t\mid S_t = s]vπ​(s)=Eπ​[Gt​∣St​=s]; they differ in how they approximate the expectation.

    TD(0) prediction

    constant-α MC:V(St)←V(St)+α[Gt−V(St)]TD(0):V(St)←V(St)+α[Rt+1+γV(St+1)⏟TD target−V(St)]\text{constant-}\alpha\text{ MC:}\quad V(S_t) \leftarrow V(S_t) + \alpha\big[G_t - V(S_t)\big] \qquad\qquad \text{TD(0):}\quad V(S_t) \leftarrow V(S_t) + \alpha\big[\underbrace{R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1})}_{\text{TD target}} - V(S_t)\big]constant-α MC:V(St​)←V(St​)+α[Gt​−V(St​)]TD(0):V(St​)←V(St​)+α[TD targetRt+1​+γV(St+1​)​​−V(St​)]
    TD error
    δt≐Rt+1+γV(St+1)−V(St),V(St)←V(St)+α δt.\delta_t \doteq R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1}) - V(S_t), \qquad V(S_t) \leftarrow V(S_t) + \alpha\,\delta_t .δt​≐Rt+1​+γV(St+1​)−V(St​),V(St​)←V(St​)+αδt​.

    The difference between the old prediction and the one-step-later prediction: a temporal difference. Many later algorithms read as "define a TD error, then take a gradient step on it".

    Where the TD target comes from

    From vπ(s)=Eπ[Gt∣St=s]v_\pi(s) = \E_\pi[G_t\mid S_t = s]vπ​(s)=Eπ​[Gt​∣St​=s] and Gt=Rt+1+γGt+1G_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma G_{t+1}Gt​=Rt+1​+γGt+1​, the tower property gives the Bellman expectation equation vπ(s)=Eπ[Rt+1+γvπ(St+1)∣St=s]v_\pi(s) = \E_\pi[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1})\mid S_t = s]vπ​(s)=Eπ​[Rt+1​+γvπ​(St+1​)∣St​=s]. Two approximations turn it into the TD target:

    • replace the expectation by a single sample (Rt+1,St+1)(R_{t+1}, S_{t+1})(Rt+1​,St+1​),
    • replace the unknown vπv_\pivπ​ by the current estimate VVV.
    Rt+1+γvπ(St+1)⏟Bellman target  ⇝  Rt+1+γV(St+1)⏟TD(0) target\underbrace{R_{t+1} + \gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1})}_{\text{Bellman target}} \;\rightsquigarrow\; \underbrace{R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1})}_{\text{TD(0) target}}Bellman targetRt+1​+γvπ​(St+1​)​​⇝TD(0) targetRt+1​+γV(St+1​)​​

    MC makes only the first approximation (with the whole return). DP makes only the second.

    Driving home (γ = 1, rewards = minutes)
    StateElapsedOld VMC targetMC errorTD targetTD error
    leaving office03043+135 + 35 = 40+10
    reach car (raining)53538+315 + 15 = 30−5
    exit highway201523+810 + 10 = 20+5
    secondary road, truck301013+310 + 3 = 13+3
    home street403303 + 0 = 30

    MC moves every prediction toward the final 43 minutes. TD moves each prediction toward the next one, and can move it the "wrong" way: at "reach car" TD lowers the estimate even though the trip ended up longer.

    Why bootstrap?

    • Over DP: no model. TD needs only sampled transitions (St,Rt+1,St+1)(S_t, R_{t+1}, S_{t+1})(St​,Rt+1​,St+1​); one observed transition stands in for the whole expectation.
    • Over MC: online and incremental. No waiting for the episode end, which matters for long episodes and continuing tasks, and every transition is used (MC control variants sometimes discard episodes after exploratory actions).
    • Sound: for fixed π\piπ, TD(0) converges in the mean for small constant α\alphaα, and with probability 1 under Robbins–Monro step sizes.
    • Often faster: no general theorem, but on stochastic problems TD usually beats constant-α MC (random walk lab below).

    Batch updating and certainty equivalence

    Batch: freeze VVV, sweep a fixed dataset accumulating Δt=α[targett−V(St)]\Delta_t = \alpha[\text{target}_t - V(S_t)]Δt​=α[targett​−V(St​)], apply the sum, repeat. For small α\alphaα, batch TD(0) and batch MC each converge to a unique fixed point independent of α\alphaα, and these points differ.

    What should V(A) be?

    Eight episodes (γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1): one is A,0,B,0A, 0, B, 0A,0,B,0; six are B,1B, 1B,1; one is B,0B, 0B,0. Everyone agrees V(B)=6/8=3/4V(B) = 6/8 = 3/4V(B)=6/8=3/4.

    • Batch MC: the only return observed from A is 0, so V(A)→0V(A) \to 0V(A)→0. Minimizes squared error on the training data.
    • Batch TD: A always went to B with reward 0, so V(A)=0+V(B)=3/4V(A) = 0 + V(B) = 3/4V(A)=0+V(B)=3/4. This is the exact answer for the maximum-likelihood Markov model of the data.
    Certainty equivalence

    Build the ML model from the data: p^(i→j)\hat p(i\to j)p^​(i→j) = fraction of observed transitions from iii that went to jjj, r^(i→j)\hat r(i\to j)r^(i→j) = their average reward. The certainty-equivalence estimate solves the Bellman equations exactly on (p^,r^)(\hat p, \hat r)(p^​,r^). Batch TD(0) converges to it, without ever building the model. Computing it directly costs O(N2)O(N^2)O(N2) memory and O(N3)O(N^3)O(N3) time; TD needs O(N)O(N)O(N) memory.

    Sarsa: on-policy TD control

    Control follows GPI, but with TD the evaluation and improvement are interleaved step by step, and we learn Q(s,a)Q(s,a)Q(s,a) so improvement is model-free. Treat each pair (St,At)(S_t, A_t)(St​,At​) as an enlarged state:

    Sarsa update
    Q(St,At)←Q(St,At)+α[Rt+1+γQ(St+1,At+1)−Q(St,At)]Q(S_t,A_t) \leftarrow Q(S_t,A_t) + \alpha\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma Q(S_{t+1},A_{t+1}) - Q(S_t,A_t)\big]Q(St​,At​)←Q(St​,At​)+α[Rt+1​+γQ(St+1​,At+1​)−Q(St​,At​)]

    Uses the quintuple (St,At,Rt+1,St+1,At+1)(S_t, A_t, R_{t+1}, S_{t+1}, A_{t+1})(St​,At​,Rt+1​,St+1​,At+1​); At+1A_{t+1}At+1​ is the action actually taken by the current (ε-greedy) policy. If St+1S_{t+1}St+1​ is terminal, the target is just Rt+1R_{t+1}Rt+1​.

    Sarsa convergence

    Needs GLIE (Greedy in the Limit with Infinite Exploration): every (s,a)(s,a)(s,a) visited infinitely often, and the policy becomes greedy w.r.t. QQQ as t→∞t \to \inftyt→∞ (e.g. ε-greedy with εt=1/t\varepsilon_t = 1/tεt​=1/t). Under GLIE and the standard step-size conditions, tabular Sarsa converges to q∗q_*q∗​ and an optimal policy.

    Q-learning: off-policy TD control

    Q-learning update
    Q(St,At)←Q(St,At)+α[Rt+1+γmax⁡aQ(St+1,a)−Q(St,At)]Q(S_t,A_t) \leftarrow Q(S_t,A_t) + \alpha\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma\max_a Q(S_{t+1},a) - Q(S_t,A_t)\big]Q(St​,At​)←Q(St​,At​)+α[Rt+1​+γamax​Q(St+1​,a)−Q(St​,At​)]

    Uses (St,At,Rt+1,St+1)(S_t, A_t, R_{t+1}, S_{t+1})(St​,At​,Rt+1​,St+1​), no At+1A_{t+1}At+1​. The target is the value of the greedy policy, whatever action is taken next. Behavior: any policy that keeps visiting all (s,a)(s,a)(s,a) (e.g. ε-greedy). Target: greedy w.r.t. QQQ. Under standard step sizes and infinite visits, Q→q∗Q \to q_*Q→q∗​ with probability 1.

    Expected Sarsa
    Q(St,At)←Q(St,At)+α[Rt+1+γ∑aπ(a∣St+1)Q(St+1,a)−Q(St,At)]Q(S_t,A_t) \leftarrow Q(S_t,A_t) + \alpha\Big[R_{t+1} + \gamma\sum_a\pi(a\mid S_{t+1})Q(S_{t+1},a) - Q(S_t,A_t)\Big]Q(St​,At​)←Q(St​,At​)+α[Rt+1​+γa∑​π(a∣St+1​)Q(St+1​,a)−Q(St​,At​)]

    Replaces the sampled At+1A_{t+1}At+1​ by its expectation under π\piπ: same mean as Sarsa, lower variance. With greedy π\piπ it is Q-learning. It appears in the slides in its n-step form.

    On-policy vs. off-policy on the cliff

    Cliff walking: −1 per step, stepping into the cliff gives −100 and a reset. Q-learning learns the values of the optimal path along the edge, but its ε-greedy behavior occasionally falls off, so its online return is worse. Sarsa learns the value of the ε-greedy policy itself, which includes those falls, and prefers the safer detour. On-policy methods evaluate what they do; off-policy methods evaluate what they would do greedily.

    Maximization bias and Double Q-learning

    The max of unbiased estimates is biased upward

    Let b∗∈arg max⁡bE[Q(s,b)]b^* \in \argmax_b \E[Q(s,b)]b∗∈argmaxb​E[Q(s,b)]. Pointwise max⁡aQ(s,a)≥Q(s,b∗)\max_a Q(s,a) \ge Q(s,b^*)maxa​Q(s,a)≥Q(s,b∗), so

    E[max⁡aQ(s,a)]≥E[Q(s,b∗)]=max⁡bE[Q(s,b)].\E\big[\max_a Q(s,a)\big] \ge \E[Q(s,b^*)] = \max_b\E[Q(s,b)].E[amax​Q(s,a)]≥E[Q(s,b∗)]=bmax​E[Q(s,b)].

    If each estimate is unbiased, the max still overestimates max⁡aq(s,a)\max_a q(s,a)maxa​q(s,a). The max preferentially selects whichever estimate has the most positive error.

    In the Q-learning target, the same table both selects A∗=arg max⁡aQ(St+1,a)A^* = \argmax_a Q(S_{t+1},a)A∗=argmaxa​Q(St+1​,a) and evaluates Q(St+1,A∗)Q(S_{t+1},A^*)Q(St+1​,A∗), so the selected positive error is preserved.

    Double Q-learning

    Keep Q1Q_1Q1​ and Q2Q_2Q2​. With probability ½ update Q1Q_1Q1​ (else symmetrically Q2Q_2Q2​):

    Q1(St,At)←Q1(St,At)+α[Rt+1+γQ2(St+1,arg max⁡aQ1(St+1,a))−Q1(St,At)]Q_1(S_t,A_t) \leftarrow Q_1(S_t,A_t) + \alpha\Big[R_{t+1} + \gamma Q_2\big(S_{t+1}, \argmax_a Q_1(S_{t+1},a)\big) - Q_1(S_t,A_t)\Big]Q1​(St​,At​)←Q1​(St​,At​)+α[Rt+1​+γQ2​(St+1​,aargmax​Q1​(St+1​,a))−Q1​(St​,At​)]

    Select with one table, evaluate with the other, whose noise is independent of the selection. Behave ε-greedily w.r.t. Q1+Q2Q_1 + Q_2Q1​+Q2​. Memory ×2, compute per step unchanged.

    Labs: random walk, cliff, maximization bias

    LabTD(0) vs. constant-α MC on the 5-state random walk

    States A–E, start at C, move left or right with probability ½, reward +1 only for exiting right, γ = 1. True values are 1/6 … 5/6; all estimates start at 0.5. The error is the RMS over the five states, averaged over runs.

    LabCliff walking: Sarsa, Expected Sarsa, Q-learning

    4 × 12 grid, start bottom-left, goal bottom-right, the bottom row between them is the cliff. α = 0.5, ε-greedy behavior. The grid shows each method's greedy path after training. Set ε to 0 and the online gap closes.

    LabMaximization bias

    From A, right ends with 0; left goes to B with 0, and every one of B's actions ends with a reward drawn from N(−0.1, 1). Going left is worse in expectation, but the max over B's noisy estimates looks positive early on. ε = 0.1, α = 0.1, γ = 1.

    Reference implementation

    import numpy as np

def eps_greedy(Q, s, eps, rng):
    if rng.random() < eps:
        return int(rng.integers(Q.shape[1]))
    q = Q[s]
    return int(rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(q == q.max())))

def td0_prediction(env, policy, n_states, episodes, alpha=0.1, gamma=1.0, rng=None):
    """env.reset() -> s ; env.step(a) -> (s2, r, done). V[terminal] is implicitly 0."""
    V = np.zeros(n_states)
    for _ in range(episodes):
        s, done = env.reset(), False
        while not done:
            s2, r, done = env.step(policy(s))
            target = r if done else r + gamma * V[s2]
            V[s] += alpha * (target - V[s])           # alpha * delta
            s = s2
    return V

def sarsa(env, nS, nA, episodes, alpha=0.5, eps=0.1, gamma=1.0, rng=None):
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    Q = np.zeros((nS, nA))
    for _ in range(episodes):
        s = env.reset(); a = eps_greedy(Q, s, eps, rng); done = False
        while not done:
            s2, r, done = env.step(a)
            if done:
                Q[s, a] += alpha * (r - Q[s, a]); break
            a2 = eps_greedy(Q, s2, eps, rng)          # the action we will actually take
            Q[s, a] += alpha * (r + gamma * Q[s2, a2] - Q[s, a])
            s, a = s2, a2
    return Q

def expected_sarsa(env, nS, nA, episodes, alpha=0.5, eps=0.1, gamma=1.0, rng=None):
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    Q = np.zeros((nS, nA))
    for _ in range(episodes):
        s, done = env.reset(), False
        while not done:
            a = eps_greedy(Q, s, eps, rng)
            s2, r, done = env.step(a)
            if done:
                target = r
            else:
                pi = np.full(nA, eps / nA)
                best = np.flatnonzero(Q[s2] == Q[s2].max())
                pi[best] += (1 - eps) / len(best)
                target = r + gamma * pi @ Q[s2]
            Q[s, a] += alpha * (target - Q[s, a])
            s = s2
    return Q

def q_learning(env, nS, nA, episodes, alpha=0.5, eps=0.1, gamma=1.0, rng=None):
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    Q = np.zeros((nS, nA))
    for _ in range(episodes):
        s, done = env.reset(), False
        while not done:
            a = eps_greedy(Q, s, eps, rng)
            s2, r, done = env.step(a)
            target = r if done else r + gamma * Q[s2].max()   # greedy target policy
            Q[s, a] += alpha * (target - Q[s, a])
            s = s2
    return Q

def double_q_learning(env, nS, nA, episodes, alpha=0.1, eps=0.1, gamma=1.0, rng=None):
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    Q1, Q2 = np.zeros((nS, nA)), np.zeros((nS, nA))
    for _ in range(episodes):
        s, done = env.reset(), False
        while not done:
            a = eps_greedy(Q1 + Q2, s, eps, rng)
            s2, r, done = env.step(a)
            A, B = (Q1, Q2) if rng.random() < 0.5 else (Q2, Q1)
            if done:
                target = r
            else:
                a_star = int(rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(A[s2] == A[s2].max())))   # select with A
                target = r + gamma * B[s2, a_star]                              # evaluate with B
            A[s, a] += alpha * (target - A[s, a])
            s = s2
    return Q1, Q2

    Gotchas and fine print

    Constant α does not converge, it hovers

    "Converges in the mean" means E[Vt]→vπ\E[V_t] \to v_\piE[Vt​]→vπ​. With a constant step size the estimates keep fluctuating around vπv_\pivπ​ forever (the lab's error curves flatten above zero). Almost-sure convergence needs decreasing, per-state step sizes satisfying the Robbins–Monro conditions.

    TD target: biased but low variance

    Rt+1+γV(St+1)R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1})Rt+1​+γV(St+1​) is biased while V≠vπV \neq v_\piV=vπ​, but depends on one random transition. GtG_tGt​ is unbiased but depends on every random action, transition and reward until the end. That trade-off, not "TD is better", is what the random-walk curves show.

    TD's error can dip and rise again

    For larger α, TD's RMS curve on the random walk falls fast and then creeps up before flattening. Part of the reason is that the initial value 0.5 is exactly right for C and the error is averaged over states; early updates move outer states quickly while the step size keeps injecting noise.

    Fixed ε finds the best ε-greedy behavior, not π*

    On the cliff with ε = 0.1, Sarsa's safe path is the right answer for an agent that keeps exploring. If you anneal ε to 0 (GLIE), Sarsa also converges to the edge path.

    Why one-step Q-learning needs no importance sampling

    Q(St,At)Q(S_t,A_t)Q(St​,At​) already conditions on AtA_tAt​, and the target max⁡aQ(St+1,a)\max_a Q(S_{t+1},a)maxa​Q(St+1​,a) is the exact expectation of Q(St+1,⋅)Q(S_{t+1},\cdot)Q(St+1​,⋅) under the greedy target policy; no behavior action after AtA_tAt​ is used. Multi-step off-policy targets do need ratios (Chapter 6).

    Double Q removes overestimation, not all bias

    The slides say the bias is "removed in expectation". More precisely, E[Q2(s,arg max⁡aQ1(s,a))]≤max⁡aq(s,a)\E[Q_2(s, \argmax_a Q_1(s,a))] \le \max_a q(s,a)E[Q2​(s,argmaxa​Q1​(s,a))]≤maxa​q(s,a): the double estimator can underestimate (van Hasselt, 2010). It removes the systematic upward bias of the max, which is what matters for the left/right example.

    Terminal states must have value 0

    A very common bug: bootstrapping from Q(terminal,⋅)Q(\text{terminal},\cdot)Q(terminal,⋅) that was accidentally updated or initialized nonzero. Either never update terminal entries or branch on done as in the code.

    Self-test

    V(s) = 2, V(s′) = 5, observed r = 1, γ = 0.9, α = 0.1. Compute δ and the new V(s).

    δ=1+0.9⋅5−2=3.5\delta = 1 + 0.9\cdot 5 - 2 = 3.5δ=1+0.9⋅5−2=3.5; V(s)=2+0.35=2.35V(s) = 2 + 0.35 = 2.35V(s)=2+0.35=2.35.

    Which two approximations turn the Bellman equation into the TD target? Which does MC make, which does DP make?

    (1) Replace the expectation by one sample; (2) replace vπv_\pivπ​ by the estimate VVV. MC samples (but uses the whole return, no VVV); DP bootstraps with VVV but computes the expectation exactly.

    Random walk A–E, V = 0.5 everywhere, α = 0.1. First episode: C → D → E → right exit. Which values change under TD(0), and to what?

    C→D: δ=0+0.5−0.5=0\delta = 0 + 0.5 - 0.5 = 0δ=0+0.5−0.5=0. D→E: δ=0\delta = 0δ=0. E→exit: δ=1+0−0.5=0.5\delta = 1 + 0 - 0.5 = 0.5δ=1+0−0.5=0.5, so V(E)=0.55V(E) = 0.55V(E)=0.55. Only E changes: TD propagates one step per episode.

    Batch TD and batch MC give different V(A) on the same data. Which is "right"?

    MC fits the observed returns (lowest training error). TD gives the certainty-equivalence answer for the ML Markov model, which is usually the better predictor of future returns if the process is Markov. If the process is not Markov, MC's answer can be better.

    Sarsa vs. Q-learning on the cliff with ε = 0.1: which has higher online return, and which learns q*?

    Sarsa has higher online return (safe path). Q-learning's Q converges toward q∗q_*q∗​ (edge path) but its ε-greedy behavior falls off the cliff sometimes, so its online return is lower.

    Show E[max⁡(X1,X2)]≥max⁡(EX1,EX2)\E[\max(X_1, X_2)] \ge \max(\E X_1, \E X_2)E[max(X1​,X2​)]≥max(EX1​,EX2​).

    max⁡(X1,X2)≥Xi\max(X_1,X_2) \ge X_imax(X1​,X2​)≥Xi​ pointwise for each iii, so Emax⁡≥EXi\E\max \ge \E X_iEmax≥EXi​ for each iii, hence ≥max⁡iEXi\ge \max_i \E X_i≥maxi​EXi​. (Jensen's inequality for the convex function max gives the same.)

    Two actions, both with true value 0, estimates independent N(0, 1). What is E[max]?

    E[max⁡(X1,X2)]=1/π≈0.564\E[\max(X_1,X_2)] = 1/\sqrt\pi \approx 0.564E[max(X1​,X2​)]=1/π​≈0.564, though both true values are 0.

    Expected Sarsa with a greedy target policy equals which algorithm?

    Q-learning: ∑aπ(a∣S′)Q(S′,a)=max⁡aQ(S′,a)\sum_a\pi(a\mid S')Q(S',a) = \max_a Q(S',a)∑a​π(a∣S′)Q(S′,a)=maxa​Q(S′,a) when π\piπ is greedy.

    Chapter 6 · Lecture 7

    n-step Bootstrapping

    One-step TD and Monte Carlo are the two ends of a dial. Use n real rewards, then bootstrap. Intermediate n usually wins, and off-policy versions need importance sampling, ideally with control variates.

    backup depth 1, 2, 3 … ∞

    The space between MC and TD

    Rt+1+γV(St+1)⏟1-step TD⋯Rt+1+⋯+γn−1Rt+n+γnV(St+n)⏟n-step⋯Rt+1+⋯+γT−t−1RT⏟Monte Carlo\underbrace{R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1})}_{\text{1-step TD}} \quad\cdots\quad \underbrace{R_{t+1} + \dots + \gamma^{n-1}R_{t+n} + \gamma^nV(S_{t+n})}_{n\text{-step}} \quad\cdots\quad \underbrace{R_{t+1} + \dots + \gamma^{T-t-1}R_T}_{\text{Monte Carlo}}1-step TDRt+1​+γV(St+1​)​​⋯n-stepRt+1​+⋯+γn−1Rt+n​+γnV(St+n​)​​⋯Monte CarloRt+1​+⋯+γT−t−1RT​​​

    n-step methods are still TD methods: they change an earlier estimate based on a later one, just nnn steps later. With one-step TD, a single time step controls two things at once: how often you can change your action, and the interval over which you bootstrap. n-step methods decouple them: act every step, bootstrap over nnn.

    n-step TD prediction

    n-step return
    Gt:t+n≐Rt+1+γRt+2+⋯+γn−1Rt+n+γnVt+n−1(St+n),n≥1, 0≤t<T−n.G_{t:t+n} \doteq R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \dots + \gamma^{n-1}R_{t+n} + \gamma^nV_{t+n-1}(S_{t+n}), \qquad n\ge1,\ 0\le t< T-n .Gt:t+n​≐Rt+1​+γRt+2​+⋯+γn−1Rt+n​+γnVt+n−1​(St+n​),n≥1, 0≤t<T−n.

    The first nnn rewards are real; everything after is replaced by the bootstrap. If t+n≥Tt+n \ge Tt+n≥T, the missing terms are 0 and Gt:t+n=GtG_{t:t+n} = G_tGt:t+n​=Gt​. Timing: Gt:t+nG_{t:t+n}Gt:t+n​ needs Rt+nR_{t+n}Rt+n​ and Vt+n−1V_{t+n-1}Vt+n−1​, which exist only at time t+nt+nt+n.

    n-step TD update
    Vt+n(St)≐Vt+n−1(St)+α[Gt:t+n−Vt+n−1(St)],0≤t<T,V_{t+n}(S_t) \doteq V_{t+n-1}(S_t) + \alpha\big[G_{t:t+n} - V_{t+n-1}(S_t)\big], \qquad 0\le t< T,Vt+n​(St​)≐Vt+n−1​(St​)+α[Gt:t+n​−Vt+n−1​(St​)],0≤t<T,

    all other states unchanged. No updates in the first n−1n-1n−1 steps of an episode; n−1n-1n−1 extra updates after termination make up for it. n=1n = 1n=1 is TD(0); n≥Tn \ge Tn≥T is constant-α MC.

    Error-reduction property
    max⁡s∣Eπ[Gt:t+n∣St=s]−vπ(s)∣≤γnmax⁡s∣Vt+n−1(s)−vπ(s)∣\max_s\Big|\E_\pi[G_{t:t+n}\mid S_t = s] - v_\pi(s)\Big| \le \gamma^n\max_s\big|V_{t+n-1}(s) - v_\pi(s)\big|smax​​Eπ​[Gt:t+n​∣St​=s]−vπ​(s)​≤γnsmax​​Vt+n−1​(s)−vπ​(s)​

    The worst error of the expected n-step return is at most γn\gamma^nγn times the worst current error. Proof sketch: the first nnn rewards are exact in expectation; the only error is in γnE[V(St+n)−vπ(St+n)]\gamma^n\E[V(S_{t+n}) - v_\pi(S_{t+n})]γnE[V(St+n​)−vπ​(St+n​)], bounded by γnmax⁡s∣V(s)−vπ(s)∣\gamma^n\max_s|V(s) - v_\pi(s)|γnmaxs​∣V(s)−vπ​(s)∣. This is why all n-step TD methods converge to vπv_\pivπ​ under the usual conditions.

    Credit after one episode

    5-state random walk, all values 0.5, first episode C → D → E → right exit (+1). 1-step: only V(E)V(E)V(E) moves toward 1. 2-step: V(D)V(D)V(D) and V(E)V(E)V(E). n>2n > 2n>2: all three visited states move toward 1, equally. Larger nnn spreads the outcome further from one episode, and over-commits to a single noisy return.

    n-step Sarsa and Expected Sarsa

    Gt:t+n≐Rt+1+⋯+γn−1Rt+n+γnQt+n−1(St+n,At+n),Qt+n(St,At)≐Qt+n−1(St,At)+α[Gt:t+n−Qt+n−1(St,At)].G_{t:t+n} \doteq R_{t+1} + \dots + \gamma^{n-1}R_{t+n} + \gamma^nQ_{t+n-1}(S_{t+n},A_{t+n}), \qquad Q_{t+n}(S_t,A_t) \doteq Q_{t+n-1}(S_t,A_t) + \alpha\big[G_{t:t+n} - Q_{t+n-1}(S_t,A_t)\big].Gt:t+n​≐Rt+1​+⋯+γn−1Rt+n​+γnQt+n−1​(St+n​,At+n​),Qt+n​(St​,At​)≐Qt+n−1​(St​,At​)+α[Gt:t+n​−Qt+n−1​(St​,At​)].

    n=1n = 1n=1 is Sarsa; n=∞n = \inftyn=∞ is MC control. When one episode reaches the only reward, one-step Sarsa strengthens only the last action; 10-step Sarsa strengthens the last ten. The second lab shows this.

    n-step Expected Sarsa
    Gt:t+n≐Rt+1+⋯+γn−1Rt+n+γnVˉt+n−1(St+n),Vˉt+n−1(s)≐∑aπ(a∣s)Qt+n−1(s,a).G_{t:t+n} \doteq R_{t+1} + \dots + \gamma^{n-1}R_{t+n} + \gamma^n\bar V_{t+n-1}(S_{t+n}), \qquad \bar V_{t+n-1}(s) \doteq \sum_a\pi(a\mid s)Q_{t+n-1}(s,a).Gt:t+n​≐Rt+1​+⋯+γn−1Rt+n​+γnVˉt+n−1​(St+n​),Vˉt+n−1​(s)≐a∑​π(a∣s)Qt+n−1​(s,a).

    The last node is an expectation over the target policy instead of a sampled action: lower variance at the last step.

If τ≥0\tau \ge 0τ≥0: G←∑i=τ+1min⁡(τ+n,T)γi−τ−1RiG \leftarrow \sum_{i=\tau+1}^{\min(\tau+n, T)}\gamma^{i-\tau-1}R_iG←∑i=τ+1min(τ+n,T)​γi−τ−1Ri​, add γnQ(Sτ+n,Aτ+n)\gamma^nQ(S_{\tau+n},A_{\tau+n})γnQ(Sτ+n​,Aτ+n​) if τ+n<T\tau + n < Tτ+n<T, update Q(Sτ,Aτ)Q(S_\tau,A_\tau)Q(Sτ​,Aτ​). Stop sampling when the episode ends, but keep updating until τ=T−1\tau = T-1τ=T−1.

    Off-policy n-step learning

    Learn about π\piπ while following bbb, reweighting by the ratio of action probabilities over the steps actually used:

    ρt:h≐∏k=tmin⁡(h,T−1)π(Ak∣Sk)b(Ak∣Sk).\rho_{t:h} \doteq \prod_{k=t}^{\min(h,T-1)}\frac{\pi(A_k\mid S_k)}{b(A_k\mid S_k)} .ρt:h​≐k=t∏min(h,T−1)​b(Ak​∣Sk​)π(Ak​∣Sk​)​.
    Vt+n(St)≐Vt+n−1(St)+αρt:t+n−1[Gt:t+n−Vt+n−1(St)],Qt+n(St,At)≐Qt+n−1(St,At)+αρt+1:t+n[Gt:t+n−Qt+n−1(St,At)].V_{t+n}(S_t) \doteq V_{t+n-1}(S_t) + \alpha\rho_{t:t+n-1}\big[G_{t:t+n} - V_{t+n-1}(S_t)\big], \qquad Q_{t+n}(S_t,A_t) \doteq Q_{t+n-1}(S_t,A_t) + \alpha\rho_{t+1:t+n}\big[G_{t:t+n} - Q_{t+n-1}(S_t,A_t)\big].Vt+n​(St​)≐Vt+n−1​(St​)+αρt:t+n−1​[Gt:t+n​−Vt+n−1​(St​)],Qt+n​(St​,At​)≐Qt+n−1​(St​,At​)+αρt+1:t+n​[Gt:t+n​−Qt+n−1​(St​,At​)].

    If π\piπ would never take one of the actions, the update is ignored. If π\piπ takes an action far more often than bbb, the return is up-weighted. If π=b\pi = bπ=b, every ratio is 1 and we recover the on-policy updates.

    Rewards −1 on the left exit and +1 on the right, γ = 1, values start at 0. Each point is the RMS error over the 19 states, averaged over the first 10 episodes and over runs. Lines are ordered from n = 1 (lightest) to n = 512 (darkest).

    LabWhich actions does one episode strengthen?

    A single episode wanders to the goal G, the only nonzero reward. With Q = 0 everywhere, n-step Sarsa raises the value of the last n actions on the path; every earlier target is still 0. Slide n.

    Reference implementation

    import numpy as np

def n_step_td(env, policy, n_states, n, alpha, episodes, gamma=1.0):
    """Tabular n-step TD prediction (Sutton & Barto, Sec. 7.1)."""
    V = np.zeros(n_states)
    for _ in range(episodes):
        S, R = [env.reset()], [0.0]                 # R[0] unused so that R[t+1] lines up
        T, t = np.inf, 0
        while True:
            if t < T:
                s2, r, done = env.step(policy(S[t]))
                S.append(s2); R.append(r)
                if done:
                    T = t + 1
            tau = t - n + 1                         # time whose estimate is updated now
            if tau >= 0:
                G = sum(gamma ** (i - tau - 1) * R[i] for i in range(tau + 1, int(min(tau + n, T)) + 1))
                if tau + n < T:
                    G += gamma ** n * V[S[tau + n]]
                V[S[tau]] += alpha * (G - V[S[tau]])
            if tau == T - 1:
                break
            t += 1
    return V

def n_step_sarsa(env, nS, nA, n, alpha=0.1, eps=0.1, gamma=1.0, episodes=100, rng=None):
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    Q = np.zeros((nS, nA))
    def act(s):
        if rng.random() < eps:
            return int(rng.integers(nA))
        return int(rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(Q[s] == Q[s].max())))
    for _ in range(episodes):
        s0 = env.reset()
        S, A, R = [s0], [act(s0)], [0.0]
        T, t = np.inf, 0
        while True:
            if t < T:
                s2, r, done = env.step(A[t])
                S.append(s2); R.append(r)
                if done:
                    T = t + 1
                else:
                    A.append(act(s2))
            tau = t - n + 1
            if tau >= 0:
                G = sum(gamma ** (i - tau - 1) * R[i] for i in range(tau + 1, int(min(tau + n, T)) + 1))
                if tau + n < T:
                    G += gamma ** n * Q[S[tau + n], A[tau + n]]
                Q[S[tau], A[tau]] += alpha * (G - Q[S[tau], A[tau]])
            if tau == T - 1:
                break
            t += 1
    return Q

def per_decision_cv_return(rewards, states, actions, V, pi, b, gamma, t, h):
    """G_{t:h} = rho_t (R_{t+1} + gamma G_{t+1:h}) + (1 - rho_t) V(S_t), computed backwards.
    rewards[k] is R_{k+1}; states/actions indexed by time; pi(a,s), b(a,s) are probabilities."""
    G = V[states[h]]                                  # bootstrap at the horizon
    for k in range(h - 1, t - 1, -1):
        rho = pi(actions[k], states[k]) / b(actions[k], states[k])
        G = rho * (rewards[k] + gamma * G) + (1 - rho) * V[states[k]]
    return G

    Gotchas and fine print

    Error reduction is about the expected return

    The γn\gamma^nγn contraction holds for Eπ[Gt:t+n]\E_\pi[G_{t:t+n}]Eπ​[Gt:t+n​], worst case over states. It shows the target points the right way; convergence of the sampled algorithm still needs stochastic-approximation conditions on α. Note also that for γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1 the bound gives nothing (the factor is 1); there, convergence relies on termination, as in DP.

    The ratio ranges differ by one step

    State values: ρt:t+n−1\rho_{t:t+n-1}ρt:t+n−1​ includes AtA_tAt​, because V(St)V(S_t)V(St​) does not condition on the first action. Sarsa: ρt+1:t+n\rho_{t+1:t+n}ρt+1:t+n​ starts after AtA_tAt​ (it is conditioned on) and includes At+nA_{t+n}At+n​, because the bootstrap Q(St+n,At+n)Q(S_{t+n},A_{t+n})Q(St+n​,At+n​) uses a sampled action. Expected Sarsa: ρt+1:t+n−1\rho_{t+1:t+n-1}ρt+1:t+n−1​, since the last node is an expectation and no action is sampled there.

    "Best n ≈ 4" is about 10 episodes

    The random-walk curves average the error over the first 10 episodes only. With more data, or a different α schedule, the best nnn changes. Large nnn needs a small α because its targets are high-variance; at large α the long-n curves leave the plot.

    Off-policy variance grows with n

    ρt:t+n−1\rho_{t:t+n-1}ρt:t+n−1​ is a product of nnn ratios, so its variance can grow exponentially in nnn, exactly like the MC example in Chapter 4. Control variates help but do not remove this. The Tree Backup algorithm (not on the slides) avoids ratios altogether by using expectations at every step.

    Off-by-one traps in the implementation

    Store Rt+1R_{t+1}Rt+1​ at index t+1t+1t+1 (keep a dummy at index 0), update time τ=t−n+1\tau = t - n + 1τ=t−n+1, and do not forget the n−1n-1n−1 flush updates after the terminal step. Missing the flush silently drops the most informative updates of each episode.

    Self-test

    γ = 0.9, rewards 1, 0, 2 over the next three steps, V(S_{t+3}) = 10. Compute Gt:t+1G_{t:t+1}Gt:t+1​, Gt:t+2G_{t:t+2}Gt:t+2​, Gt:t+3G_{t:t+3}Gt:t+3​ given V(S_{t+1}) = 4, V(S_{t+2}) = 6.

    Gt:t+1=1+0.9⋅4=4.6G_{t:t+1} = 1 + 0.9\cdot4 = 4.6Gt:t+1​=1+0.9⋅4=4.6. Gt:t+2=1+0+0.81⋅6=5.86G_{t:t+2} = 1 + 0 + 0.81\cdot6 = 5.86Gt:t+2​=1+0+0.81⋅6=5.86. Gt:t+3=1+0+0.81⋅2+0.729⋅10=9.91G_{t:t+3} = 1 + 0 + 0.81\cdot2 + 0.729\cdot10 = 9.91Gt:t+3​=1+0+0.81⋅2+0.729⋅10=9.91.

    What are the two extreme members of the n-step family?

    n=1n = 1n=1: one-step TD (Sarsa for control). n=∞n = \inftyn=∞ (or n≥Tn \ge Tn≥T): Monte Carlo.

    Why can't the n-step update for StS_tSt​ happen at time t+1?

    The target needs Rt+nR_{t+n}Rt+n​ and V(St+n)V(S_{t+n})V(St+n​), which are only observed at time t+nt+nt+n.

    Prove the error-reduction bound in one line.

    E[Gt:t+n∣St=s]−vπ(s)=γnE[V(St+n)−vπ(St+n)∣St=s]\E[G_{t:t+n}\mid S_t=s] - v_\pi(s) = \gamma^n\E[V(S_{t+n}) - v_\pi(S_{t+n})\mid S_t = s]E[Gt:t+n​∣St​=s]−vπ​(s)=γnE[V(St+n​)−vπ​(St+n​)∣St​=s] (the reward terms cancel against those inside vπv_\pivπ​). Its absolute value is at most γnmax⁡s′∣V(s′)−vπ(s′)∣\gamma^n\max_{s'}|V(s') - v_\pi(s')|γnmaxs′​∣V(s′)−vπ​(s′)∣.

    π(a|s) = 0.9 for the action b took with probability 0.3, then π = 0.1 for an action b took with probability 0.5. What is ρ over these two steps?

    (0.9/0.3)(0.1/0.5)=3⋅0.2=0.6(0.9/0.3)(0.1/0.5) = 3\cdot0.2 = 0.6(0.9/0.3)(0.1/0.5)=3⋅0.2=0.6.

    Why does the control-variate term (1−ρt)V(St)(1-\rho_t)V(S_t)(1−ρt​)V(St​) not bias the target?

    Given StS_tSt​, V(St)V(S_t)V(St​) is a constant and Eb[ρt∣St]=1\E_b[\rho_t\mid S_t] = 1Eb​[ρt​∣St​]=1, so Eb[(1−ρt)V(St)∣St]=0\E_b[(1-\rho_t)V(S_t)\mid S_t] = 0Eb​[(1−ρt​)V(St​)∣St​]=0.

    A single episode reaches the only reward after 20 steps. How many Q-values does one-step Sarsa change, and how many does 10-step Sarsa change (Q = 0 initially)?

    One-step: only the last pair. 10-step: the last 10 pairs, since only their targets include the reward (earlier targets are sums of zeros plus bootstraps from zero-valued Q).

    Chapter 7 · Lecture 8

    Planning and Learning with Tabular Methods

    Planning is learning from imagined experience. A learned model turns each real step into many updates (Dyna), search control decides which ones, and decision-time planning spends all its effort on the move in front of you (rollouts, MCTS).

    real and simulated backups

    Models and planning

    Model-free methods (MC, TD) and model-based methods (DP, search) both improve value estimates by backing up information from the future. They differ mainly in where the experience comes from.

    Distribution model vs. sample model

    A model is anything the agent can use to predict what follows a state and action. A distribution model gives all outcomes with probabilities, p^(s′,r∣s,a)\hat p(s',r\mid s,a)p^​(s′,r∣s,a); DP needs this. A sample model produces one sampled (S′,R)(S', R)(S′,R); it is easier to obtain and to simulate from (think of a game engine).

    Planning

    Any computation that takes a model as input and produces or improves a policy: model → simulated experience → backups → better policy.
