    Dyna: integrating acting, learning and planning

    Dyna learns from real experience, learns a model from the same experience, uses the model to simulate more experience, and learns again from that. Four pieces: acting, direct RL, model learning, planning, plus search control, which picks the state–action pairs to simulate.

    Tabular Dyna-Q, per real step
    1. Choose AAA from SSS ε-greedily on QQQ; execute, observe R,S′R, S'R,S′.
    2. Direct RL: Q(S,A)←Q(S,A)+α[R+γmax⁡aQ(S′,a)−Q(S,A)]Q(S,A) \leftarrow Q(S,A) + \alpha[R + \gamma\max_aQ(S',a) - Q(S,A)]Q(S,A)←Q(S,A)+α[R+γmaxa​Q(S′,a)−Q(S,A)].
    3. Model learning: M^(S,A)←(R,S′)\hat M(S,A) \leftarrow (R, S')M^(S,A)←(R,S′) (deterministic environment assumed).
    4. Planning, nnn times: pick a previously seen (s~,a~)(\tilde s,\tilde a)(s~,a~) at random, get (r~,s~′)=M^(s~,a~)(\tilde r,\tilde s') = \hat M(\tilde s,\tilde a)(r~,s~′)=M^(s~,a~), apply the same Q-learning update.
    5. S←S′S \leftarrow S'S←S′.

    Same backup for real and simulated experience; only the source differs.

    Planning lets learning race ahead of the agent

    Without planning, after two episodes only the cell next to the goal has a nonzero value. With 50 planning steps per real step, value has already propagated back over most of the route while the agent is still near the start. The Dyna maze lab shows both.

    When the model is wrong

    Models go wrong because the environment is stochastic, data is limited, approximation generalizes badly, or the environment changes. A bad model makes planning compute a bad policy faster.

    • Blocking maze (the old short path closes): the model predicts transitions that now fail; acting on them reveals the error, so plain Dyna-Q eventually adapts.
    • Shortcut maze (a new short path opens): the model says there is no shortcut, planning keeps reinforcing the old route, and plain Dyna-Q may never find it. Trusting an outdated model suppresses the exploration needed to repair it.
    Dyna-Q+: computational curiosity

    Track τ(s,a)\tau(s,a)τ(s,a), the number of time steps since (s,a)(s,a)(s,a) was last tried for real. During planning, use the reward

    r+=r+κτ(s,a).r^+ = r + \kappa\sqrt{\tau(s,a)} .r+=r+κτ(s,a)​.

    Long-untried actions look attractive, so the agent goes back to check parts of the world it has neglected. It explores to test whether its model has gone stale, not only for reward.

    Prioritized sweeping

    Uniform random planning updates waste effort: early on most do nothing, and when one state's value changes, only its predecessors are immediately affected. Prioritized sweeping works backward from change:

    • keep a priority queue of state–action pairs, keyed by the size of their Bellman error P=∣R+γmax⁡aQ(S′,a)−Q(S,A)∣P = |R + \gamma\max_aQ(S',a) - Q(S,A)|P=∣R+γmaxa​Q(S′,a)−Q(S,A)∣;
    • pop the most urgent pair, update it;
    • for every predecessor (sˉ,aˉ)(\bar s,\bar a)(sˉ,aˉ) predicted to lead to it, compute its error and push it if above a threshold.

    Search control matters as much as the update rule itself.

    Expected vs. sample updates

    expected: Q(s,a)←∑s′,rp^(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γmax⁡a′Q(s′,a′)]sample: Q(s,a)←Q(s,a)+α[R+γmax⁡a′Q(S′,a′)−Q(s,a)]\text{expected: } Q(s,a) \leftarrow \sum_{s',r}\hat p(s',r\mid s,a)\big[r + \gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\big] \qquad \text{sample: } Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha\big[R + \gamma\max_{a'}Q(S',a') - Q(s,a)\big]expected: Q(s,a)←s′,r∑​p^​(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γa′max​Q(s′,a′)]sample: Q(s,a)←Q(s,a)+α[R+γa′max​Q(S′,a′)−Q(s,a)]

    Expected updates are exact given the model; sample updates are noisy but cheaper. With branching factor bbb (number of possible next states), one expected update costs about as much as bbb sample updates. If the successor values are already correct, ttt sample updates with α=1/t\alpha = 1/tα=1/t leave an error of about (b−1)/(bt)\sqrt{(b-1)/(bt)}(b−1)/(bt)​ times the initial error. For large bbb, a fraction of bbb sample updates removes most of the error. When computation is the bottleneck, sample updates often win. The third lab plots this.

    Trajectory sampling and RTDP

    Prioritized sweepingTrajectory sampling
    Directionbackward from states whose value changedforward from the current state along the policy
    CriterionBellman-error magnitudeon-policy visitation
    Goalpropagate new information to predecessorsconcentrate compute on states the agent reaches
    Mottofix what is most wrong firstwork on what is most relevant

    On-policy trajectory sampling usually wins early; uniform sweeps can catch up on small problems. On large problems, focusing where the policy goes can be a big advantage.

    Real-time dynamic programming (RTDP)

    Asynchronous value iteration along trajectories. For each trial start at an initial state and, until terminal: act greedily, A∈arg max⁡a∑s′,rp^(s′,r∣S,a)[r+γV(s′)]A \in \argmax_a\sum_{s',r}\hat p(s',r\mid S,a)[r + \gamma V(s')]A∈argmaxa​∑s′,r​p^​(s′,r∣S,a)[r+γV(s′)]; update V(S)←max⁡a∑s′,rp^(s′,r∣S,a)[r+γV(s′)]V(S) \leftarrow \max_a\sum_{s',r}\hat p(s',r\mid S,a)[r + \gamma V(s')]V(S)←maxa​∑s′,r​p^​(s′,r∣S,a)[r+γV(s′)]; move on. DP does expected backups over all states; RTDP does them only along sampled trajectories.

    Decision-time planning

    Background planning (Dyna) improves a value function or policy that is reused across many states. Decision-time planning plans specifically for the current state, uses the result to pick one action now, and starts over at the next step.

    Heuristic search

    Search forward from the current state, expand a look-ahead tree selectively, evaluate leaves with a heuristic v^\hat vv^, back values up to the root, choose the best root action.

    Backing up a small tree (γ = 1)

    Root sss with actions a1a_1a1​ (leading to xxx) and a2a_2a2​ (truncated, v^=4\hat v = 4v^=4). At xxx: b1b_1b1​ leads to mmm, b2b_2b2​ is truncated with v^=6\hat v = 6v^=6. At mmm: stochastic action o1o_1o1​ gives 12 or 2 with probability ½ each, o2o_2o2​ gives 5.

    E[o1]=0.5⋅12+0.5⋅2=7,v(m)=max⁡(7,5)=7,v(x)=max⁡(7,6)=7,Q(s,a1)=7>Q(s,a2)=4.\E[o_1] = 0.5\cdot12 + 0.5\cdot2 = 7,\quad v(m) = \max(7,5) = 7,\quad v(x) = \max(7,6) = 7,\quad Q(s,a_1) = 7 > Q(s,a_2) = 4.E[o1​]=0.5⋅12+0.5⋅2=7,v(m)=max(7,5)=7,v(x)=max(7,6)=7,Q(s,a1​)=7>Q(s,a2​)=4.

    Bottom-up, the operators alternate: average at stochastic nodes, max at decision nodes. Selective depth is what makes it heuristic search.

    Rollout algorithms

    Decision-time Monte Carlo planning: for each action aaa available now, simulate KKK trajectories that start with aaa and then follow a fixed rollout policy π\piπ; estimate q^(s,a)=1K∑iG(i)\hat q(s,a) = \frac1K\sum_iG^{(i)}q^​(s,a)=K1​∑i​G(i); pick the best. No global value function is learned.

    Monte Carlo tree search

    MCTS keeps and refines statistics in a partial search tree rooted at the current state. Each node stores a visit count NNN and a mean value QQQ; the tree grows by one node per iteration, and uses a tree policy inside the tree and a rollout policy beyond its frontier. One iteration:

    1. Select: descend from the root with the tree policy to a node with an untried action.
    2. Expand: add one child node.
    3. Simulate: roll out to the end with the rollout policy, get return GGG.
    4. Backup: along the selected path, N+=1N \mathrel{+}= 1N+=1 and Q←Q+1N(G−Q)Q \leftarrow Q + \frac1N(G - Q)Q←Q+N1​(G−Q). The rollout itself is not stored.

    After the budget, play arg max⁡aN(s0,a)\argmax_aN(s_0,a)argmaxa​N(s0​,a), the most-visited root action rather than the one with the best mean: the tree policy already steers simulations toward promising moves, so a high count is a robust signal while a high QQQ on few visits may be luck. Then observe s′s's′, keep the subtree under the move taken as the new root, and plan again.

    The space of updates

    Horizontal axis: sample vs. expected updates. Vertical axis: shallow vs. deep. Dyna-Q is a one-step sample update; RTDP and DP are one-step expected updates; rollout and MCTS are deep sampled trajectories; heuristic search is deep and selective, bootstrapping its leaves. The backup shape hides search control: two methods with the same diagram can update different states in a different order.

    LabExpected vs. sample updates

    Error remaining in one Q estimate as a function of computation, measured in units of one expected update (bbb successor evaluations). Expected updates do nothing until all bbb successors are summed; sample updates improve immediately.

    Reference implementation

    import heapq, math, random
import numpy as np

def dyna_q(env, nS, nA, steps, n_plan=10, alpha=0.1, gamma=0.95, eps=0.1,
           kappa=0.0, rng=None):
    """Dyna-Q (kappa = 0) or Dyna-Q+ (kappa > 0). Deterministic model M[(s,a)] = (r, s2, done)."""
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    Q, M, last_tried, seen = np.zeros((nS, nA)), {}, {}, set()
    s = env.reset()
    for t in range(steps):
        a = int(rng.integers(nA)) if rng.random() < eps else int(rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(Q[s] == Q[s].max())))
        s2, r, done = env.step(a)
        Q[s, a] += alpha * (r + (0 if done else gamma * Q[s2].max()) - Q[s, a])     # direct RL
        if kappa and s not in seen:                     # Dyna-Q+: untried actions modeled as
            for b in range(nA):                         # "stay put, reward 0" until really tried
                M.setdefault((s, b), (0.0, s, False)); last_tried.setdefault((s, b), t)
        seen.add(s)
        M[(s, a)] = (r, s2, done); last_tried[(s, a)] = t                         # model learning
        keys = list(M)
        for _ in range(n_plan):                                                   # planning
            ps, pa = keys[rng.integers(len(keys))]
            pr, ps2, pdone = M[(ps, pa)]
            pr += kappa * math.sqrt(t - last_tried[(ps, pa)])                     # curiosity bonus
            Q[ps, pa] += alpha * (pr + (0 if pdone else gamma * Q[ps2].max()) - Q[ps, pa])
        s = env.reset() if done else s2
    return Q

def prioritized_sweeping(env, nS, nA, steps, n_plan=5, alpha=0.1, gamma=0.95, eps=0.1, theta=1e-4, rng=None):
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    Q, M, preds, pq = np.zeros((nS, nA)), {}, {}, []
    s = env.reset()
    for _ in range(steps):
        a = int(rng.integers(nA)) if rng.random() < eps else int(np.argmax(Q[s]))
        s2, r, done = env.step(a)
        M[(s, a)] = (r, s2, done); preds.setdefault(s2, set()).add((s, a))
        P = abs(r + (0 if done else gamma * Q[s2].max()) - Q[s, a])
        if P > theta:
            heapq.heappush(pq, (-P, (s, a)))
        for _ in range(n_plan):
            if not pq:
                break
            _, (ps, pa) = heapq.heappop(pq)
            pr, ps2, pdone = M[(ps, pa)]
            Q[ps, pa] += alpha * (pr + (0 if pdone else gamma * Q[ps2].max()) - Q[ps, pa])
            for (bs, ba) in preds.get(ps, ()):          # push predecessors of the changed state
                br, _, _ = M[(bs, ba)]
                Pb = abs(br + gamma * Q[ps].max() - Q[bs, ba])
                if Pb > theta:
                    heapq.heappush(pq, (-Pb, (bs, ba)))
        s = env.reset() if done else s2
    return Q

class Node:
    def __init__(self, state, parent=None):
        self.state, self.parent, self.children, self.N, self.W = state, parent, {}, 0, 0.0
    def Q(self):
        return self.W / self.N if self.N else 0.0

def mcts(root_state, model, actions, budget=1000, c=1.4, rollout_depth=50, gamma=1.0):
    """UCT. model(s, a) -> (s2, r, done) is a sample model; actions(s) -> legal actions.
    Single-agent version (rewards from one player's perspective)."""
    root = Node(root_state)
    for _ in range(budget):
        node, path_reward, discount, done = root, 0.0, 1.0, False
        # 1. selection
        while node.children and len(node.children) == len(actions(node.state)) and not done:
            a, node = max(node.children.items(),
                          key=lambda kv: kv[1].Q() + c * math.sqrt(math.log(node.N + 1) / (kv[1].N + 1e-9)))
            _, r, done = model(node.parent.state, a)   # deterministic model assumed: replay edge reward
            path_reward += discount * r; discount *= gamma
        # 2. expansion
        if not done:
            untried = [a for a in actions(node.state) if a not in node.children]
            if untried:
                a = random.choice(untried)
                s2, r, done = model(node.state, a)
                path_reward += discount * r; discount *= gamma
                node.children[a] = Node(s2, node); node = node.children[a]
        # 3. simulation with a uniform rollout policy
        s, G = node.state, 0.0
        for _ in range(rollout_depth):
            if done:
                break
            s, r, done = model(s, random.choice(actions(s)))
            G += discount * r; discount *= gamma
        # 4. backup (incremental means via W / N)
        total = path_reward + G
        while node is not None:
            node.N += 1; node.W += total; node = node.parent
    return max(root.children, key=lambda a: root.children[a].N)   # most visited, not best mean

    Gotchas and fine print

    Dyna-Q's model is one sample per pair

    M^(s,a)←(R,S′)\hat M(s,a) \leftarrow (R, S')M^(s,a)←(R,S′) stores the last outcome. That is a correct model only for deterministic environments. In a stochastic one, planning replays whatever happened last, which biases QQQ; you would store counts (a distribution model) or all observed outcomes instead.

    Planning only revisits what it has seen

    Dyna-Q samples previously observed pairs, so the model never imagines unvisited transitions. The textbook Dyna-Q+ additionally lets planning consider never-tried actions from visited states, modeled as leading back to the same state with reward 0; without that, the bonus cannot draw the agent toward truly untried actions.

    The bonus lives in planning, not in the real reward

    Dyna-Q+ adds κτ\kappa\sqrt\tauκτ​ to simulated rewards only. The real environment and the direct-RL update are unchanged. The bonus does distort QQQ (it is no longer an estimate of q∗q_*q∗​), which costs some reward in a static world; that is the "exploratory cost" in the method map.

    MCTS selection is UCB from Chapter 1

    The usual tree policy (UCT) picks children by Q+cln⁡N(parent)/N(child)Q + c\sqrt{\ln N(\text{parent})/N(\text{child})}Q+clnN(parent)/N(child)​: the bandit UCB rule applied at every node. The slides leave the tree policy abstract.

    Rollout improves on the rollout policy, no more

    With exact estimates, choosing arg max⁡aq^π(s,a)\argmax_a\hat q_\pi(s,a)argmaxa​q^​π​(s,a) is one step of policy improvement over the rollout policy π\piπ at the current state (policy improvement theorem). A bad rollout policy gives a better-but-still-bad decision. MCTS goes further because its tree policy changes as statistics accumulate.

    RTDP's exploration comes from optimistic values

    RTDP acts greedily and never explores at random. Its guarantee (converging to optimal values on the relevant states without visiting all states) needs conditions such as an undiscounted episodic task and initial values that are optimistic, so that greedy behavior is drawn to unvisited states.

    The error formula assumes correct successor values

    (b−1)/(bt)\sqrt{(b-1)/(bt)}(b−1)/(bt)​ compares one expected update against ttt sample updates when the values of the successors are already right. In real planning they are also being learned, which tends to favour sample updates even more: early, fast, partial updates make the successor values better sooner.

    Self-test

    Distribution model vs. sample model: which does DP need, which does Dyna-Q use?

    DP needs a distribution model to compute expectations. Dyna-Q uses a (deterministic) sample model: one stored outcome per pair.

    Why does Dyna-Q with n = 50 solve the maze in far fewer episodes than n = 0, even though both see the same real data?

    Each real transition is replayed many times through the model, so the goal's value propagates backward over many states per real step instead of one state per episode.

    Why does plain Dyna-Q adapt to the blocking maze but miss the shortcut?

    Blocking: the old path fails when the agent tries it, so real experience corrects the model. Shortcut: the old path still works, the model never contains the new transitions, and planning keeps making the old path look best, so the agent has no reason to explore the new one.

    κ = 0.01. A transition untried for 2500 steps: what is the bonus?

    0.012500=0.50.01\sqrt{2500} = 0.50.012500​=0.5.

    Branching factor b = 100. Roughly what fraction of the initial error remains after 25 sample updates vs. after zero and one full expected update?

    Sample: 99/(100⋅25)≈0.199\sqrt{99/(100\cdot25)} \approx 0.19999/(100⋅25)​≈0.199, about 20%. Expected update: 100% until all 100 successors are evaluated, then 0. The 25 sample updates cost a quarter of one expected update.

    Prioritized sweeping vs. trajectory sampling: what does each prioritize?

    Prioritized sweeping: pairs with large Bellman error, propagating backward to predecessors. Trajectory sampling: states the current policy actually visits, forward from the current state.

    MCTS picks the most visited root action instead of the highest Q. Why?

    The tree policy already concentrates visits on actions that look good, so the visit count aggregates a lot of evidence. A high Q on few visits may be lucky noise.

    Heuristic search: change the stochastic outcome at m to 12 / −4 (prob. ½ each). Which root action is chosen now?

    E[o1]=4\E[o_1] = 4E[o1​]=4, v(m)=max⁡(4,5)=5v(m) = \max(4, 5) = 5v(m)=max(4,5)=5, v(x)=max⁡(5,6)=6v(x) = \max(5, 6) = 6v(x)=max(5,6)=6, so Q(s,a1)=6>4Q(s,a_1) = 6 > 4Q(s,a1​)=6>4: still a1a_1a1​, now because of the truncated leaf v^=6\hat v = 6v^=6 under b2b_2b2​.

    Chapter 8 · Lecture 9

    On-Policy Prediction with Function Approximation

    When almost every state is new, a table is useless. Replace it with v^(s,w)\hat v(s,\mathbf w)v^(s,w), choose an objective, follow its (semi-)gradient, design features, and learn which combinations stay stable: linear and on-policy is safe, the deadly triad is not.

    features → weights → value

    Why tables break

    Tabular RL stores one number per state and works only if every relevant state is visited many times. Real states are continuous (sensors, joint angles), high-dimensional (images) or combinatorial (positions of many objects). An 84 × 84 grayscale image has 25684⋅84=2567056256^{84\cdot84} = 256^{7056}25684⋅84=2567056 configurations. Two problems: the table cannot be stored, and most states are seen at most once, so even free memory would not help.

    Generalization is the central issue

    Experience in some states must inform predictions in many others. Function approximation gives a compact representation and controlled sharing of information across states.

    Parameterized value functions

    v^(s,w)≈vπ(s),w∈Rd, d≪∣S∣.\hat v(s,\mathbf w) \approx v_\pi(s), \qquad \mathbf w\in\R^d,\ d \ll |\S| .v^(s,w)≈vπ​(s),w∈Rd, d≪∣S∣.

    One weight change affects predictions in many states, so generalization is automatic, and so is interference: reducing the error at one state cannot leave all others untouched. Approximators: linear in features v^=w⊤x(s)\hat v = \mathbf w^\top\mathbf x(s)v^=w⊤x(s), neural networks, trees, kernel methods.

    The s↦us \mapsto us↦u view. Every prediction update says "the value at StS_tSt​ should look more like UtU_tUt​". MC: Ut=GtU_t = G_tUt​=Gt​. TD(0): Ut=Rt+1+γv^(St+1,w)U_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma\hat v(S_{t+1},\mathbf w)Ut​=Rt+1​+γv^(St+1​,w). n-step: Ut=Gt:t+nU_t = G_{t:t+n}Ut​=Gt:t+n​. DP: Ut=Eπ[Rt+1+γv^(St+1,w)∣St]U_t = \E_\pi[R_{t+1} + \gamma\hat v(S_{t+1},\mathbf w)\mid S_t]Ut​=Eπ​[Rt+1​+γv^(St+1​,w)∣St​]. RL produces a stream of training pairs; the approximator fits them. Unlike supervised learning, we compute the labels ourselves.

    Why this is harder than regression: learning is online; data comes from π\piπ's visitation distribution (correlated, uneven); with bootstrapping the label moves as the weights move; in control the policy and hence the data distribution change too.

    The prediction objective

    Mean-squared value error
    VE‾(w)≐∑sμ(s)[vπ(s)−v^(s,w)]2,μ(s)≥0, ∑sμ(s)=1.\VE(\mathbf w) \doteq \sum_s\mu(s)\big[v_\pi(s) - \hat v(s,\mathbf w)\big]^2, \qquad \mu(s)\ge0,\ \sum_s\mu(s) = 1 .VE(w)≐s∑​μ(s)[vπ​(s)−v^(s,w)]2,μ(s)≥0, s∑​μ(s)=1.

    μ\muμ is the on-policy distribution: in a continuing task (ergodic chain) the long-run fraction of time spent in sss; in an episodic task it also depends on the start-state distribution. Changing where episodes start changes μ\muμ, and so changes what counts as a good approximation.

    The TD fixed point (linear, on-policy)

    In expectation, the linear semi-gradient TD(0) update is E[Δw]=α(b−Aw)\E[\Delta\mathbf w] = \alpha(\mathbf b - \mathbf A\mathbf w)E[Δw]=α(b−Aw) with

    Feature construction

    The representable functions are exactly span⁡{x1(⋅),…,xd(⋅)}\operatorname{span}\{x_1(\cdot),\dots,x_d(\cdot)\}span{x1​(⋅),…,xd​(⋅)}. If vπv_\pivπ​ lies outside, no w\mathbf ww recovers it. Two design questions: capacity (can the basis express the regularities?) and generalization (which states should share parameters?). Use domain knowledge: spatial features for a robot's position; angle, angular velocity and their product for pole balancing.

    • State aggregation: partition states into groups, one weight per group, xi(s)=1[s∈group i]x_i(s) = \mathbb 1[s\in\text{group }i]xi​(s)=1[s∈group i]. The gradient is one-hot; groups do not interact; v^\hat vv^ is a staircase.
    • Fourier cosine basis: for s∈[0,1]k\mathbf s\in[0,1]^ks∈[0,1]k and frequency vectors c∈{0,…,n}k\mathbf c\in\{0,\dots,n\}^kc∈{0,…,n}k, xc(s)=cos⁡(πc⊤s)x_{\mathbf c}(\mathbf s) = \cos(\pi\mathbf c^\top\mathbf s)xc​(s)=cos(πc⊤s); (n+1)k(n+1)^k(n+1)k features. A zero entry ignores that dimension, larger entries oscillate faster, the ratio sets the orientation. Per-feature step size αi=α/∥c(i)∥2\alpha_i = \alpha/\|\mathbf c^{(i)}\|_2αi​=α/∥c(i)∥2​ (α\alphaα for c=0\mathbf c = 0c=0).
    • Coarse coding: binary features for overlapping regions. An update at sss moves the weights of all active features, affecting every state that shares them, in proportion to the number of shared features. E.g. regions [0,0.3],[0.2,0.5],[0.4,0.7],[0.6,0.9],[0.8,1][0,0.3],[0.2,0.5],[0.4,0.7],[0.6,0.9],[0.8,1][0,0.3],[0.2,0.5],[0.4,0.7],[0.6,0.9],[0.8,1]: x(0.45)=(0,1,1,0,0)⊤\mathbf x(0.45) = (0,1,1,0,0)^\topx(0.45)=(0,1,1,0,0)⊤ and v^(0.45)=w2+w3\hat v(0.45) = w_2 + w_3v^(0.45)=w2​+w3​. Wide regions generalize broadly early; final accuracy depends mostly on the number of features.
    • Tile coding: nnn offset tilings, each a partition into tiles; exactly one active tile per tiling, so nnn active binary features. Step size α=1/(τn)\alpha = 1/(\tau n)α=1/(τn) moves the prediction by about 1/τ1/\tau1/τ of the error. Hashing keeps memory bounded.
    • Radial basis functions: xi(s)=exp⁡(−∥s−ci∥2/(2σi2))x_i(s) = \exp(-\|s - c_i\|^2/(2\sigma_i^2))xi​(s)=exp(−∥s−ci​∥2/(2σi2​)): smooth, differentiable coarse coding; expensive and of limited help in high dimensions.

    State aggregationtrivial, exact gradientcoarse staircase

    Choosing features often matters more than choosing the algorithm. With memory fixed at 1000 weights, 50 offset tilings of 20 tiles each beat one tiling of 1000 tiles on the 1000-state random walk: nearby states share many active tiles, far ones few.

    Nonlinear approximation: neural networks

    Linear methods are limited by hand-made features; high-dimensional inputs need representation learning. Power goes up, theory and stability go down.

    • A unit computes z=w⊤x+bz = \mathbf w^\top\mathbf x + bz=w⊤x+b, a=ϕ(z)a = \phi(z)a=ϕ(z) with sigmoid, tanh or ReLU max⁡(0,z)\max(0,z)max(0,z).
    • Nonlinearity is mandatory: without it, LLL layers collapse to one affine map (∏W(ℓ))a(0)+b~\big(\prod W^{(\ell)}\big)\mathbf a^{(0)} + \tilde{\mathbf b}(∏W(ℓ))a(0)+b~.
    • Universal approximation (Cybenko 1989): one hidden layer with enough sigmoid units approximates any continuous function on a compact set. Expressiveness is not the bottleneck; optimization is.
    • Training uses the same rule w←w+αδt∇v^(St,w)\mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w + \alpha\delta_t\nabla\hat v(S_t,\mathbf w)w←w+αδt​∇v^(St​,w), with the gradient from backpropagation.
    The deadly triad

    Function approximation (updates couple), bootstrapping (targets depend on w\mathbf ww) and off-policy learning (the update distribution is not the on-policy one): together they can make TD-style updates diverge. Any two are fine. The Baird lab below shows the divergence with a perfectly representable value function.

    Adaptive optimizers (Adam, RMSProp) do not replace stable targets and good scaling; they can hide instability until values suddenly explode. Dropout helps supervised learning but adds noise to already noisy bootstrapped targets.

    Case study: DQN

    Mnih et al. (2015): one network per Atari game, same architecture and hyperparameters for all 49 games, input = raw pixels and score. A single frame is not Markov (no motion), so the state ϕ\phiϕ stacks the last 4 grayscale 84 × 84 frames. One forward pass outputs Q(s,a;w)Q(s,a;\mathbf w)Q(s,a;w) for every action. ε-greedy during training (ε from 1.0 down to 0.1), ε = 0.05 at evaluation.

    DQN update
    Y=Rclipped+γmax⁡a′Q(S′,a′;w−),w←w+α[Y−Q(S,A;w)]∇wQ(S,A;w).Y = R^{\text{clipped}} + \gamma\max_{a'}Q(S',a';\mathbf w^-), \qquad \mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w + \alpha\big[Y - Q(S,A;\mathbf w)\big]\nabla_{\mathbf w}Q(S,A;\mathbf w).Y=Rclipped+γa′max​Q(S′,a′;w−),w←w+α[Y−Q(S,A;w)]∇w​Q(S,A;w).

    Replay buffer N=106N = 10^6N=106, target refresh every C=104C = 10^4C=104 steps, γ=0.99\gamma = 0.99γ=0.99, minibatch 32, rewards clipped to {−1,0,+1}\{-1,0,+1\}{−1,0,+1}, error clipping with RMSProp.

    DQN is off-policy: the target policy is greedy (the max), and the buffer holds data from ε-greedy versions of older networks. It sits squarely in the deadly triad; replay (decorrelation, reuse) and the target network (a fixed target between refreshes, turning the step into ordinary regression) are what make it work. Result: at least 75% of a professional tester's score on 29 of 49 games; strongest on reactive games, near zero on Montezuma's Revenge, where sparse delayed reward defeats ε-greedy exploration.

    Reference implementation

    import numpy as np

class TileCoder1D:
    """n offset tilings over [lo, hi]; each tiling has `tiles` tiles (+1 for the offset overhang)."""
    def __init__(self, n_tilings=50, tiles=20, lo=0.0, hi=1.0):
        self.n, self.tiles, self.lo, self.width = n_tilings, tiles, lo, (hi - lo) / tiles
        self.d = n_tilings * (tiles + 1)
    def active(self, s):
        idx = []
        for k in range(self.n):
            offset = k * self.width / self.n
            idx.append(k * (self.tiles + 1) + int((s - self.lo + offset) // self.width))
        return np.array(idx)

def fourier_features(s, order):            # s in [0,1]^k
    s = np.atleast_1d(s)
    C = np.array(np.meshgrid(*[range(order + 1)] * len(s))).reshape(len(s), -1).T
    return np.cos(np.pi * C @ s), C

def gradient_mc(episodes, feat, d, alpha):
    """episodes: list of (states, G) with gamma = 1 and a single terminal reward."""
    w = np.zeros(d)
    for states, G in episodes:
        for s in states:
            x = feat(s)
            w += alpha * (G - w @ x) * x
    return w

def semi_gradient_td0(env, policy, feat, d, alpha, episodes, gamma=1.0):
    w = np.zeros(d)
    for _ in range(episodes):
        s, done = env.reset(), False
        while not done:
            s2, r, done = env.step(policy(s))
            x = feat(s)
            target = r if done else r + gamma * w @ feat(s2)     # target treated as a constant
            w += alpha * (target - w @ x) * x
            s = s2
    return w

def td_fixed_point(transitions, feat, gamma):
    """Solve A w = b from on-policy samples (LSTD): A = E[x (x - gamma x')^T], b = E[r x]."""
    xs = [feat(s) for s, r, s2, done in transitions]
    d = len(xs[0]); A = np.zeros((d, d)); b = np.zeros(d)
    for (s, r, s2, done), x in zip(transitions, xs):
        x2 = np.zeros(d) if done else feat(s2)
        A += np.outer(x, x - gamma * x2); b += r * x
    return np.linalg.solve(A + 1e-6 * np.eye(d), b)

# --- DQN skeleton (PyTorch) -------------------------------------------------
def dqn_update(q_net, target_net, optimizer, batch, gamma=0.99, double=False):
    import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
    s, a, r, s2, done = batch                          # tensors from the replay buffer
    q = q_net(s).gather(1, a.unsqueeze(1)).squeeze(1)
    with torch.no_grad():                              # semi-gradient: no grad through the target
        if double:
            a2 = q_net(s2).argmax(1, keepdim=True)     # online net selects
            q2 = target_net(s2).gather(1, a2).squeeze(1)   # target net evaluates
        else:
            q2 = target_net(s2).max(1).values
        y = r.clamp(-1, 1) + gamma * (1 - done.float()) * q2
    loss = F.smooth_l1_loss(q, y)                      # Huber loss = clipped TD error
    optimizer.zero_grad(); loss.backward()
    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(q_net.parameters(), 10.0)
    optimizer.step()
    return loss.item()

    Gotchas and fine print

    Semi-gradient TD is not gradient descent on anything

    In general there is no objective whose gradient is the semi-gradient update. That is why "SGD converges to a local minimum" does not transfer. In the linear on-policy case the expected update α(b−Aw)\alpha(\mathbf b - \mathbf A\mathbf w)α(b−Aw) is a stable linear system because A\mathbf AA is positive definite under μ\muμ; off-policy, A\mathbf AA can have eigenvalues with negative real part, and the iteration diverges.

    The 1/(1−γ) bound gets loose fast

    At γ=0.99\gamma = 0.99γ=0.99 the TD fixed point may have up to 100 times the minimal VE‾\VEVE. TD's lower variance often wins in practice anyway, but asymptotically it can be noticeably worse than MC.

    State aggregation fits μ-weighted group averages

    Gradient MC with aggregation converges to wg=∑s∈gμ(s)vπ(s)/∑s∈gμ(s)w_g = \sum_{s\in g}\mu(s)v_\pi(s)/\sum_{s\in g}\mu(s)wg​=∑s∈g​μ(s)vπ​(s)/∑s∈g​μ(s), not the plain average of vπv_\pivπ​ over the group. Near the edges, where μ\muμ is small and skewed, the steps are visibly distorted. Look at the end groups in the lab.

    VE is the prediction objective, not the control objective

    Lower VE‾\VEVE does not imply a better policy. In control the value function is only useful insofar as it ranks actions correctly in the states that matter.

    Step size scales with the number of active features

    With nnn active binary features, one update changes v^(s)\hat v(s)v^(s) by αn δ\alpha n\,\deltaαnδ. That is why tile coding uses α=1/(τn)\alpha = 1/(\tau n)α=1/(τn). In general α=(τ E[x⊤x])−1\alpha = (\tau\,\E[\mathbf x^\top\mathbf x])^{-1}α=(τE[x⊤x])−1.

    Universal approximation says "exists", not "learnable"

    It guarantees a network with small error exists; it says nothing about how many units, how much data, or whether SGD finds it.

    Replay makes DQN off-policy even with ε = 0

    The buffer mixes transitions from older networks, so the data distribution is never that of the current greedy policy. The target network does not create a convergence guarantee; it removes the fastest feedback loop.

    Uniform tile offsets create diagonal artifacts

    In more than one dimension, offsetting every tiling by the same amount in every dimension makes generalization favour the diagonal. The textbook recommends asymmetric displacement vectors such as (1,3,5,… )(1, 3, 5, \dots)(1,3,5,…) times a unit.

    Self-test

    Why is μ in the objective, and what happens if you change the start-state distribution?

    With fewer parameters than states we cannot be exact everywhere, so we weight errors by how often π\piπ visits each state. Changing where episodes start changes μ\muμ, and so changes which approximation is "best".

    Write the linear semi-gradient TD(0) update and say what is treated as constant.

    w←w+α[R+γw⊤x′−w⊤x]x\mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w + \alpha[R + \gamma\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x' - \mathbf w^\top\mathbf x]\mathbf xw←w+α[R+γw⊤x′−w⊤x]x. The target R+γw⊤x′R + \gamma\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x'R+γw⊤x′ is treated as a constant; only the gradient of the prediction, x\mathbf xx, is used.

    Gradient MC is true SGD. Why isn't semi-gradient TD?

    Its target depends on w\mathbf ww and is biased while v^≠vπ\hat v \ne v_\piv^=vπ​. Ignoring the target's dependence on w\mathbf ww means the update is not the gradient of VE‾\VEVE (or of any fixed objective in general).

    γ = 0.9 and the best linear approximation has VE = 0.02. What does the bound guarantee for TD?

    VE‾(wTD)≤0.02/(1−0.9)=0.2\VE(\mathbf w_{TD}) \le 0.02/(1-0.9) = 0.2VE(wTD​)≤0.02/(1−0.9)=0.2.

    Coarse coding regions [0,0.3], [0.2,0.5], [0.4,0.7], [0.6,0.9], [0.8,1]. Which weights does an update at s = 0.65 change, and does it affect s = 0.45?

    s=0.65s = 0.65s=0.65 lies in regions 3 and 4, so w3,w4w_3, w_4w3​,w4​. s=0.45s = 0.45s=0.45 uses w2,w3w_2, w_3w2​,w3​: it shares w3w_3w3​, so yes, half as strongly as a state sharing both.

    Tile coding with 8 tilings, and you want each update to move the prediction about 1/10 of the error. Which α?

    α=1/(τn)=1/(10⋅8)=0.0125\alpha = 1/(\tau n) = 1/(10\cdot8) = 0.0125α=1/(τn)=1/(10⋅8)=0.0125.

    Name the three legs of the deadly triad and show which DQN tricks address which leg.

    Function approximation, bootstrapping, off-policy learning. The target network tames the bootstrapping leg (targets stop moving between refreshes); replay is the source of off-policy data but decorrelates samples; double estimators reduce overestimation from the max. None removes a leg entirely.

    Why does DQN stack 4 frames?

    One frame does not show velocity or direction, so it is not a Markov state. Four frames approximately are.

    Chapter 9 · Lecture 10

    Policy Gradient Methods

    Parameterize the policy itself and climb the gradient of expected return. The policy gradient theorem makes that gradient computable from samples; REINFORCE, baselines and actor–critic are three ways to estimate it.

    shape a distribution over actions

    Why parameterize the policy

    So far: learn q(s,a)q(s,a)q(s,a), then act greedily or ε-greedily. Now: parameterize π(a∣s,θ)≐Pr⁡{At=a∣St=s,θt=θ}\pi(a\mid s,\boldsymbol\theta) \doteq \Pr\{A_t = a\mid S_t = s,\boldsymbol\theta_t = \boldsymbol\theta\}π(a∣s,θ)≐Pr{At​=a∣St​=s,θt​=θ}, θ∈Rd′\boldsymbol\theta\in\R^{d'}θ∈Rd′, choose a scalar performance measure J(θ)J(\boldsymbol\theta)J(θ) and ascend it: θt+1=θt+α∇J(θt)^\boldsymbol\theta_{t+1} = \boldsymbol\theta_t + \alpha\widehat{\nabla J(\boldsymbol\theta_t)}θt+1​=θt​+α∇J(θt​)​. A value function may still help learn θ\boldsymbol\thetaθ, but is not needed to act.

    • Approach determinism smoothly. ε-greedy always keeps ε of random actions; a parameterized policy can drive the optimal action's probability to 1.
    • Represent stochastic optima. Under function approximation or partial observability the best policy may be stochastic (bluffing in poker; the short corridor below).
    • Simpler object. Sometimes a policy is easier to represent than q∗q_*q∗​.
    • Continuous actions come naturally (Gaussian policies).

    The difficulty: performance depends on the action probabilities and on the state distribution they induce, which depends on the unknown environment. Computing the gradient looks like it needs a model.

    Softmax in action preferences

    π(a∣s,θ)≐eh(s,a,θ)∑beh(s,b,θ),h(s,a,θ)=θ⊤x(s,a) (linear)  or a neural network.\pi(a\mid s,\boldsymbol\theta) \doteq \frac{e^{h(s,a,\boldsymbol\theta)}}{\sum_be^{h(s,b,\boldsymbol\theta)}}, \qquad h(s,a,\boldsymbol\theta) = \boldsymbol\theta^\top\mathbf x(s,a)\ \text{(linear)}\ \text{ or a neural network.}π(a∣s,θ)≐∑b​eh(s,b,θ)eh(s,a,θ)​,h(s,a,θ)=θ⊤x(s,a) (linear)  or a neural network.

    Preferences are relative (adding a constant to all preferences in a state changes nothing), so the optimal action's preference can keep growing and π(a∗∣s)→1\pi(a^*\mid s) \to 1π(a∗∣s)→1 without a temperature schedule. Unlike ε-greedy, whose probabilities jump discontinuously at the decision boundary and take only two levels, softmax moves π\piπ continuously with θ\boldsymbol\thetaθ, which is what gradient ascent needs.

    Short corridor with switched actions

    Three non-terminal states, actions left/right, reward −1 per step, γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1. In the middle state the actions are reversed. All states share the features x(s,right)=[1,0]⊤\mathbf x(s,\text{right}) = [1,0]^\topx(s,right)=[1,0]⊤, x(s,left)=[0,1]⊤\mathbf x(s,\text{left}) = [0,1]^\topx(s,left)=[0,1]⊤, so any policy picks right with the same probability ppp everywhere. ε-greedy can only realize p∈{ε/2,1−ε/2}p\in\{\varepsilon/2, 1-\varepsilon/2\}p∈{ε/2,1−ε/2}; for ε=0.1\varepsilon = 0.1ε=0.1 the better of the two gets about −44. The best stochastic policy has p≈0.59p\approx0.59p≈0.59 and gets about −11.6. Stochasticity here is the optimum, not exploration noise. The first lab plots J(p)J(p)J(p).

    The policy gradient theorem

    Episodic objective with a fixed start state: J(θ)≐vπθ(s0)=Eπθ[∑t=0T−1γtRt+1∣S0=s0]J(\boldsymbol\theta) \doteq v_{\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}}(s_0) = \E_{\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}}\big[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^tR_{t+1}\mid S_0 = s_0\big]J(θ)≐vπθ​​(s0​)=Eπθ​​[∑t=0T−1​γtRt+1​∣S0​=s0​].

    Policy gradient theorem (episodic)
    ∇J(θ)∝∑sμ(s)∑aqπ(s,a)∇π(a∣s,θ)=ES∼μ, A∼π[qπ(S,A)∇ln⁡π(A∣S,θ)],\nabla J(\boldsymbol\theta) \propto \sum_s\mu(s)\sum_aq_\pi(s,a)\nabla\pi(a\mid s,\boldsymbol\theta) = \E_{S\sim\mu,\,A\sim\pi}\big[q_\pi(S,A)\nabla\ln\pi(A\mid S,\boldsymbol\theta)\big],∇J(θ)∝s∑​μ(s)a∑​qπ​(s,a)∇π(a∣s,θ)=ES∼μ,A∼π​[qπ​(S,A)∇lnπ(A∣S,θ)],

    where μ\muμ is the on-policy state distribution under πθ\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}πθ​. No derivative of the state distribution appears: only how θ\boldsymbol\thetaθ changes the action probabilities. Sample where the policy goes and what it does, then raise ln⁡π\ln\pilnπ in proportion to qπq_\piqπ​.

    Proof

    1. Product rule. From vπ(s)=∑aπ(a∣s)qπ(s,a)v_\pi(s) = \sum_a\pi(a\mid s)q_\pi(s,a)vπ​(s)=∑a​π(a∣s)qπ​(s,a):

    ∇vπ(s)=∑a[∇π(a∣s) qπ(s,a)⏟action selection+π(a∣s) ∇qπ(s,a)⏟future value].\nabla v_\pi(s) = \sum_a\Big[\underbrace{\nabla\pi(a\mid s)\,q_\pi(s,a)}_{\text{action selection}} + \underbrace{\pi(a\mid s)\,\nabla q_\pi(s,a)}_{\text{future value}}\Big].∇vπ​(s)=a∑​[action selection∇π(a∣s)qπ​(s,a)​​+future valueπ(a∣s)∇qπ​(s,a)​​].

    2. Bellman for qπq_\piqπ​. ppp and rrr do not depend on θ\boldsymbol\thetaθ, so ∇qπ(s,a)=γ∑s′p(s′∣s,a)∇vπ(s′)\nabla q_\pi(s,a) = \gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\nabla v_\pi(s')∇qπ​(s,a)=γ∑s′​p(s′∣s,a)∇vπ​(s′).

    3. A Bellman-style recursion for the gradient. With ϕ(s)≐∑a∇π(a∣s)qπ(s,a)\phi(s) \doteq \sum_a\nabla\pi(a\mid s)q_\pi(s,a)ϕ(s)≐∑a​∇π(a∣s)qπ​(s,a) and Pπ(s′∣s)=∑aπ(a∣s)p(s′∣s,a)P_\pi(s'\mid s) = \sum_a\pi(a\mid s)p(s'\mid s,a)Pπ​(s′∣s)=∑a​π(a∣s)p(s′∣s,a),

    Case study: AlphaGo

    Go: 19 × 19 board, about 250 legal moves per turn over roughly 150 moves, around 1017010^{170}10170 positions, and positions are hard to evaluate by hand. As an MDP: state = board, actions = legal moves, reward ±1 at the end. AlphaGo (Silver et al., 2016) beat Fan Hui 5–0 and Lee Sedol 4–1.

    NetworkTrained howRole
    pπp_\pipπ​ rolloutsupervised, linear softmaxfast move sampling in MCTS rollouts (~24% accuracy)
    pσp_\sigmapσ​ SL policysupervised on ~30M expert movesprior for MCTS (~57%)

    To move, AlphaGo runs thousands of MCTS simulations: the policy network proposes moves worth looking at, the value network (mixed with rollouts) judges the resulting positions, and the search decides by accumulating those judgments. The SL policy, not the stronger RL policy, gave the better MCTS prior because it is more diverse; the RL policy's real job was producing data for the value network.

    LabOne update, by hand

    Set the parameters, the sampled action and the return; see the eligibility vector and the new policy.

    Reference implementation

    import numpy as np

def softmax(h):
    z = np.exp(h - h.max()); return z / z.sum()

class SoftmaxLinearPolicy:
    def __init__(self, feat, n_actions, d, rng=None):
        self.feat, self.nA, self.theta = feat, n_actions, np.zeros(d)   # feat(s, a) -> R^d
        self.rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    def probs(self, s):
        return softmax(np.array([self.theta @ self.feat(s, a) for a in range(self.nA)]))
    def sample(self, s):
        return int(self.rng.choice(self.nA, p=self.probs(s)))
    def grad_log(self, s, a):
        p = self.probs(s)
        return self.feat(s, a) - sum(p[b] * self.feat(s, b) for b in range(self.nA))

def run_episode(env, policy, max_steps=10_000):
    S, A, R = [], [], []
    s, done = env.reset(), False
    while not done and len(S) < max_steps:
        a = policy.sample(s); s2, r, done = env.step(a)
        S.append(s); A.append(a); R.append(r); s = s2
    return S, A, R

def returns(R, gamma):
    G, out = 0.0, np.zeros(len(R))
    for t in reversed(range(len(R))):
        G = R[t] + gamma * G; out[t] = G
    return out

def reinforce(env, policy, episodes, alpha=2**-13, gamma=1.0):
    for _ in range(episodes):
        S, A, R = run_episode(env, policy)
        for t, G in enumerate(returns(R, gamma)):
            policy.theta += alpha * gamma ** t * G * policy.grad_log(S[t], A[t])

def reinforce_baseline(env, policy, v_feat, dv, episodes, a_theta=2**-9, a_w=2**-6, gamma=1.0):
    w = np.zeros(dv)
    for _ in range(episodes):
        S, A, R = run_episode(env, policy)
        for t, G in enumerate(returns(R, gamma)):
            x = v_feat(S[t])
            delta = G - w @ x                                     # advantage estimate
            w += a_w * delta * x
            policy.theta += a_theta * gamma ** t * delta * policy.grad_log(S[t], A[t])
    return w

def one_step_actor_critic(env, policy, v_feat, dv, episodes, a_theta=2**-9, a_w=2**-6, gamma=1.0):
    w = np.zeros(dv)
    for _ in range(episodes):
        s, done, I = env.reset(), False, 1.0
        while not done:
            a = policy.sample(s); s2, r, done = env.step(a)
            v2 = 0.0 if done else w @ v_feat(s2)
            delta = r + gamma * v2 - w @ v_feat(s)                # TD error = advantage estimate
            w += a_w * delta * v_feat(s)
            policy.theta += a_theta * I * delta * policy.grad_log(s, a)
            I *= gamma; s = s2
    return w

def gaussian_grad_log(a, x_mu, x_sigma, theta_mu, theta_sigma):
    """Eligibility vectors of a Gaussian policy with linear mean and log-linear std."""
    mu, sigma = theta_mu @ x_mu, np.exp(theta_sigma @ x_sigma)
    g_mu = (a - mu) / sigma**2 * x_mu
    g_sigma = ((a - mu)**2 / sigma**2 - 1.0) * x_sigma
    return g_mu, g_sigma

class ShortCorridor:
    """States 0,1,2 nonterminal; action 1 = right, 0 = left; in state 1 the actions are swapped."""
    def reset(self):
        self.s = 0; return 0
    def step(self, a):
        move = (1 if a == 1 else -1) * (-1 if self.s == 1 else 1)
        self.s = max(0, self.s + move)
        return self.s, -1.0, self.s == 3

feat = lambda s, a: np.array([1.0, 0.0]) if a == 1 else np.array([0.0, 1.0])
pol = SoftmaxLinearPolicy(feat, 2, 2); pol.theta = np.array([-1.47, 1.47])  # pi(right) ~ 0.05
reinforce_baseline(ShortCorridor(), pol, lambda s: np.array([1.0]), 1, episodes=1000)
print(pol.probs(0))    # [pi(left), pi(right)]; hovers around [0.41, 0.59] but keeps
                       # fluctuating (pi(right) roughly 0.45-0.75) because the step sizes are constant

    Gotchas and fine print

    Dropping γᵗ changes the direction

    Many implementations use Gt∇ln⁡πG_t\nabla\ln\piGt​∇lnπ without the γt\gamma^tγt factor. For a discounted objective that is not the gradient of JJJ; it is a biased direction that weights late time steps too heavily (Thomas, 2014). It often works fine in practice, but it is a different algorithm.

    Which μ? The discounted one

    In the proof, μ\muμ is the normalized discounted visitation η(x)=∑kγkPr⁡(s0→x,k)\eta(x) = \sum_k\gamma^k\Pr(s_0\to x,k)η(x)=∑k​γkPr(s0​→x,k). Sampling states uniformly from trajectories (undiscounted visitation) matches it only when γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1; the γt\gamma^tγt in REINFORCE is what corrects for this.

    The baseline may depend on the state, never on the action

    The proof uses ∑ab(s)∇π(a∣s)=0\sum_ab(s)\nabla\pi(a\mid s) = 0∑a​b(s)∇π(a∣s)=0, which needs bbb constant across actions. A baseline that depends on AtA_tAt​ biases the gradient.

    The TD error is an unbiased advantage only with the true value

    E[δt∣St,At]=qπ(St,At)−v^(St)\E[\delta_t\mid S_t,A_t] = q_\pi(S_t,A_t) - \hat v(S_t)E[δt​∣St​,At​]=qπ​(St​,At​)−v^(St​) requires v^(St+1)\hat v(S_{t+1})v^(St+1​) to equal vπ(St+1)v_\pi(S_{t+1})vπ​(St+1​) in expectation. With an inaccurate critic, actor–critic follows a biased direction; with REINFORCE + baseline, v^\hat vv^ only affects the variance.

    A critic that cannot tell states apart is badly biased

    In the short corridor the features alias all states, so a state-value critic is one number www. Its TD error is δ=−1+w−w=−1\delta = -1 + w - w = -1δ=−1+w−w=−1 on every intermediate step and −1−w-1 - w−1−w on the last one. Every action except the one that ends the episode gets pushed down, which drives π(right)→1\pi(\text{right}) \to 1π(right)→1, where the corridor never ends. Monte Carlo REINFORCE with the same scalar baseline works fine, because the baseline only affects variance.

    The score-function identity needs π > 0

    ∇π=π∇ln⁡π\nabla\pi = \pi\nabla\ln\pi∇π=π∇lnπ requires positive probabilities. Softmax guarantees that; a deterministic optimum is reached only in the limit ∥θ∥→∞\|\boldsymbol\theta\|\to\infty∥θ∥→∞, and gradient ascent slows down as probabilities saturate.

    Convergence is to a local optimum

    J(θ)J(\boldsymbol\theta)J(θ) is not concave in general. REINFORCE guarantees a local optimum at best; the short corridor happens to have a single optimum in ppp.

    Step size is the main hyperparameter

    In the corridor, α=2−12\alpha = 2^{-12}α=2−12 is too aggressive, 2−132^{-13}2−13 converges, 2−142^{-14}2−14 is slow. The baseline allows a much larger actor step (2−92^{-9}2−9), which is most of where its speedup comes from.

    Self-test

    Why can't an ε-greedy action-value method find the best policy in the short corridor?

    The features make all states look identical, so a deterministic greedy policy chooses the same action everywhere and ε-greedy can only realize p∈{ε/2,1−ε/2}p\in\{\varepsilon/2, 1-\varepsilon/2\}p∈{ε/2,1−ε/2}. The best policy needs p≈0.59p \approx 0.59p≈0.59.

    The derivative of the state distribution with respect to θ\boldsymbol\thetaθ. Unrolling the gradient recursion collects all of it into the visitation weights η(x)\eta(x)η(x), which on-policy sampling provides for free.

    REINFORCE + baseline vs. actor–critic: which is biased and which can learn online?

    REINFORCE + baseline is unbiased but must wait for GtG_tGt​ (episode end). Actor–critic bootstraps with v^(St+1)\hat v(S_{t+1})v^(St+1​), so it learns online but is biased while the critic is wrong.

    Gaussian policy with μ = 0, σ = 1. Sampled a = 2 with positive advantage. Which way do the mean and the spread move?

    ∂ln⁡π/∂μ=(a−μ)/σ2=2>0\partial\ln\pi/\partial\mu = (a-\mu)/\sigma^2 = 2 > 0∂lnπ/∂μ=(a−μ)/σ2=2>0: the mean moves toward 2. The σ\sigmaσ term is (a−μ)2/σ2−1=3>0(a-\mu)^2/\sigma^2 - 1 = 3 > 0(a−μ)2/σ2−1=3>0: the spread grows, because a good action was found far from the mean.

    In AlphaGo, why was the SL policy used as the MCTS prior instead of the stronger RL policy?

    It is more diverse: it spreads probability over more plausible moves, which suits a search prior. The RL policy is sharper and better at playing directly, and its main use was generating self-play data for the value network.

    Chapter 10 · Summary lecture

    One Idea, Many Algorithms

    One problem (the MDP), one principle (Bellman consistency), one update rule with different targets. Three questions place any algorithm: what is learned, what is the target, and whose data is it?

    Why incremental?

    The expectation is over unknown dynamics, so we can only sample it. Stepping α toward each noisy target averages the noise out (stochastic approximation). Updates cost O(1)O(1)O(1) in time and memory, run online, and a constant α tracks moving targets: an improving policy, shifting bootstrap values.

    The space of updates

    Width: average over all successors (needs ppp) or sample one (needs only experience)? Depth: back up one step and bootstrap, or wait for the full return? DP, MC and TD are corners of one continuous space. n-step methods fill the depth edge; Dyna moves toward the expected side by learning a model; exhaustive search is the far corner. Hover the points in the map below.

    The algorithm family tree

    • Value-based (learn vvv or qqq, act greedily)
      • model known or learned: DP (policy and value iteration), Dyna, MCTS
      • model-free, tabular: MC control; Sarsa, Q-learning, n-step Sarsa
      • model-free, approximate: semi-gradient Sarsa, DQN
    • Policy-based (learn π(a∣s,θ)\pi(a\mid s,\boldsymbol\theta)π(a∣s,θ) directly): REINFORCE (± baseline); actor–critic (critic = TD value learning)

    GPI: the engine of all control

    Policy iterationrepeated DP sweeps to vπv_\pivπ​greedy
    Value iterationone DP backupimplicit max
    MC controlepisode returnsε-greedy

    Evaluation makes values consistent with the policy; improvement makes the policy greedy with respect to the values; their only joint fixed point is optimality. Policy gradients replace greedification by gradient ascent on J(θ)J(\boldsymbol\theta)J(θ): actor–critic keeps the interplay (GPI in spirit), REINFORCE has no evaluation step at all.

    Recurring trade-offs
    • Bias vs. variance: bootstrapping (TD, small n, critics) vs. full returns (MC, large n, REINFORCE).
    • Samples vs. compute: model-free learning vs. planning with a model (Dyna, MCTS).
    • Exploration vs. exploitation: ε-greedy, optimism, UCB, Dyna-Q+ bonuses, stochastic policies.
    • Stability: the deadly triad (function approximation + bootstrapping + off-policy) can diverge without safeguards.

    Reference implementation

    import numpy as np

def target(kind, t, S, R, V, gamma, n=None, pi=None, Q=None, A=None, p=None):
    """Every value-learning target in the course for the state (or pair) at time t.
    S[t]: states, R[t+1]: reward after step t (R[0] unused), T = len(S) - 1 is terminal.
    V: state values (V[terminal] = 0). Q: action values. pi(a, s): target policy. p(s): model."""
    T = len(S) - 1
    if kind == "mc":
        return sum(gamma ** (k - t - 1) * R[k] for k in range(t + 1, T + 1))
    if kind == "td0":
        return R[t + 1] + gamma * V[S[t + 1]]
    if kind == "nstep":
        h = min(t + n, T)
        G = sum(gamma ** (k - t - 1) * R[k] for k in range(t + 1, h + 1))
        return G + (gamma ** n * V[S[t + n]] if t + n < T else 0.0)
    if kind == "dp":                       # expected update through a model p(s) -> [(prob, r, s2)]
        return sum(prob * (r + gamma * V[s2]) for prob, r, s2 in p(S[t]))
    if kind == "sarsa":
        return R[t + 1] + gamma * Q[S[t + 1], A[t + 1]]
    if kind == "qlearning":
        return R[t + 1] + gamma * Q[S[t + 1]].max()
    if kind == "expected_sarsa":
        s2 = S[t + 1]
        return R[t + 1] + gamma * sum(pi(a, s2) * Q[s2, a] for a in range(Q.shape[1]))
    raise ValueError(kind)

def update(V, s, tgt, alpha):
    V[s] += alpha * (tgt - V[s])           # the one rule: new = old + alpha (target - old)

    Cross-cutting gotchas

    "Converges" always comes with conditions

    Tabular TD and Q-learning: every pair visited infinitely often and Robbins–Monro step sizes. Sarsa: GLIE as well. Linear semi-gradient TD: on-policy distribution. Policy gradients: a local optimum. Contraction arguments: γ<1\gamma < 1γ<1, or proper policies when γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1. When a statement says "converges", ask which of these it assumed.

    Two kinds of "off-policy correction"

    One-step Q-learning needs no importance ratio; MC, n-step and λ\lambdaλ off-policy methods do. DQN is off-policy through its max target and replay, and uses no ratios at all, which is part of why it lives in the deadly triad.

    On-policy "evaluates what it does"

    Sarsa's values include the cost of its own exploration; Q-learning's do not. When comparing learning curves, check whether they report online return (behavior policy) or the greedy policy's return.

    Baselines vs. critics

    A baseline subtracts a state-dependent number and leaves the expected gradient unchanged. A critic replaces the return by a bootstrapped estimate, which changes the expected update and adds bias. REINFORCE with v^\hat vv^ as baseline is not an actor–critic method.

    The same backup diagram can hide very different algorithms

    Dyna-Q, prioritized sweeping and Q-learning all use the one-step sample max backup. They differ in where the transitions come from and in which order they are backed up: search control.

    Exam-style self-test

    Place Q-learning, REINFORCE and Dyna-Q by the three questions: what is learned, what is the target, whose data?

    Q-learning: learns QQQ; target R+γmax⁡aQ(S′,a)R + \gamma\max_aQ(S',a)R+γmaxa​Q(S′,a); off-policy (data from ε-greedy, target greedy). REINFORCE: learns πθ\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}πθ​; "target" is the return GtG_tGt​ weighting ∇ln⁡π\nabla\ln\pi∇lnπ; on-policy. Dyna-Q: learns QQQ and a model; same Q-learning target on real and simulated transitions; off-policy.

    γ = 1. Episode: S₀ → S₁ → S₂ → terminal, rewards 0, 0, 1. V(S₁) = 0.3, V(S₂) = 0.6. Targets for V(S₀): TD(0), 2-step, MC?

    TD(0): 0+0.3=0.30 + 0.3 = 0.30+0.3=0.3. 2-step: 0+0+0.6=0.60 + 0 + 0.6 = 0.60+0+0.6=0.6. MC: 0+0+1=10 + 0 + 1 = 10+0+1=1.

    Which methods in this course bootstrap? Which use a model?

    Bootstrap: DP, TD(0), n-step TD (finite n), Sarsa, Q-learning, Expected Sarsa, Dyna, semi-gradient TD, DQN, actor–critic. No bootstrap: MC, REINFORCE (with or without baseline), rollout. Model: DP (given), Dyna and prioritized sweeping (learned), RTDP, heuristic search, rollout, MCTS (sample model or simulator).

    Explain why the cliff makes Sarsa and Q-learning differ, using the words on-policy and off-policy.

    Sarsa is on-policy: its target uses the action the ε-greedy policy actually takes next, so its values account for occasional random steps into the cliff and it prefers the safe path. Q-learning is off-policy: it learns the greedy policy's values (edge path) while behaving ε-greedily, so its online returns suffer from falls.

    Name the deadly triad and one algorithm in the course that has all three legs.

    Function approximation, bootstrapping, off-policy learning. DQN (and semi-gradient off-policy TD on Baird's example).

    Bias–variance: rank MC, n-step TD with n = 4, TD(0) from lowest to highest variance of the target.

    TD(0) < 4-step < MC in variance; the reverse order in bias (while the value estimates are wrong).

    Which algorithms in the table are GPI, and which is the exception?

    Policy iteration, value iteration, MC control, Sarsa, Q-learning, Dyna-Q are GPI with different evaluation steps; actor–critic is GPI in spirit with gradient ascent instead of greedification. REINFORCE has no evaluation step and is the exception.

    When would you choose a policy-gradient method over Q-learning?

    Continuous or very large action spaces (no max over actions needed); when the best representable policy is stochastic (aliased states, partial observability, games); when you want smooth changes in behavior; or when the policy is simpler to represent than the value function.
